cards.question: Name the **five** common AI capabilities that developers can integrate into an application when planning an Azure AI solution.
cards.answer:
- **Generative AI and agents** — LLMs that generate original responses to prompts; agents add instructions and tools
- **Natural language processing** — making sense of language in text
- **Computer speech** — recognizing and synthesizing speech
- **Computer vision** — interpreting images, video and live camera streams
- **Information extraction** — pulling key information out of documents, forms, images and recordings
cards.explanation: Today's AI solutions are built on machine learning models that capture semantic relationships found in huge amounts of data. That lets an app appear to interpret input, reason over it and generate responses or predictions. Choosing the capabilities comes first in planning: it tells you which AI services you must provision, configure and use. Information extraction is the combined one, drawing on generative AI, language, vision and speech together.

cards.question: Generative AI is increasingly the foundation for **agentic AI**. Which **three** things does an AI agent combine, and what does each add?
cards.answer:
- **LLM** — generates original responses to natural language prompts
- **Instructions** — focused, define the agent's task responsibilities
- **Tools** — let the agent find relevant knowledge and automate its tasks
cards.explanation: Plain generative AI answers prompts: it powers interactive chat applications and AI-assisted content creation. An agent builds on that rather than replacing it. The instructions narrow the LLM to the job the agent is responsible for. The tools give it a way to look up relevant knowledge and to carry out the tasks, so it automates work instead of only producing text.

cards.question: A grocery store wants an automated checkout that identifies which products are in a customer's basket, so nobody has to scan a barcode or type in product and quantity. Which AI capability does it need?
cards.answer: **Computer vision**.
cards.explanation: Computer vision lets AI apps and agents accept, interpret and process visual input from images, videos and live camera streams. At the checkout the camera view of the basket is the input, and recognizing the products in it is the task. There is no text to analyze, no voice to recognize and no document to read.

options.why: It interprets visual input such as a camera stream and identifies the products in it.
It pulls key fields out of documents, forms and recordings, such as the total from a receipt, not products from a live scene.
NLP makes sense of text such as documents, emails and social media messages; there is no text here.
It recognizes and synthesizes spoken language; the checkout works from images, not voice.

cards.question: An expense claims app must pull the purchase date, line items and total cost out of scanned receipts. Which AI capability is this, and which **three** kinds of AI does it combine?
cards.answer:
**Information extraction**, combining:
- **Generative AI** models for language reasoning
- **Natural language** techniques for document understanding
- **Computer vision and speech** for media analysis
cards.explanation: Information extraction is not one technique but a mix of the others. A scanned receipt is an image, so vision reads it; language techniques understand it as a document; a generative model reasons over the content. The same combination extracts key information from forms, images, recordings and other content, which is why speech belongs to it too.

cards.question: Generative AI LLMs can now perform many common natural language processing (NLP) tasks. In which area can specialized NLP still pay off, and with which **two** kinds of techniques?
cards.answer:
Specialized **text analysis**, using:
- **Term-frequency** algorithms (statistical NLP)
- **Task-specific models** for text classification, sentiment analysis and summarization
cards.explanation: Modern LLMs grew out of NLP, a long-established area of AI that uses statistical and semantic models to make sense of language in documents, emails, social media messages and other text. Most everyday language tasks can now go to an LLM. Specialized text analysis is the exception: counting how often terms occur, or a model built for one task, can still serve it better.

cards.question: Which **two** of these solutions depend on the computer speech capability?
cards.answer: **Transcribing and analyzing** recorded calls, and a **"read aloud"** feature that synthesizes speech from text.
cards.explanation: Computer speech works in both directions: recognizing speech and synthesizing it. Besides voice conversations with apps and agents, it is a core part of transcribing and analyzing live or recorded speech, and of turning text into speech for simultaneous translation or read-aloud interfaces. Recent advances let it cope with background noise, interruptions, and many languages and accents.

options.text: Transcribing and analyzing recorded customer support calls
options.why: Transcription and analysis of live or recorded speech is a core use of speech recognition.

options.text: A "read aloud" feature that speaks a web article to the user
options.why: Synthesizing speech from text is the other half of computer speech.

options.text: Scoring the sentiment of written product reviews
options.why: This is text analysis, a natural language processing task; no audio is involved.

options.text: Identifying products in a shopping basket from a camera feed
options.why: Interpreting camera streams is computer vision.

cards.question: What makes a generative AI model **multimodal** with respect to visual content?
cards.answer: It can both **process visual input** and **generate visual output** in the form of images and videos.
cards.explanation: Computer vision on its own only reads visual content: it accepts, interprets and processes images, videos and live camera streams, as when a grocery checkout recognizes the products in a basket. Generative AI models are increasingly multimodal, and that closes the loop. A model that interprets a picture is no longer limited to working with what it sees; it can also create new visual content.

cards.question: Your team must create and manage Microsoft Foundry project assets from **automated CI/CD actions in a DevOps pipeline**. What do you use?
cards.answer: The **Microsoft Foundry SDK**, which builds and manages assets programmatically. Its visual counterpart is the **Microsoft Foundry portal**, the web-based interface for working with projects by hand.
cards.explanation: Most projects start in the portal: there you find, compare, deploy and test models, create and test agents, create MCP connections to tools and Foundry IQ knowledge sources, explore Foundry Tools, manage resource configuration and user access, and look up endpoints and keys. As soon as these operations must run from scripts or pipelines, the SDK automates them.

options.why: It creates and manages project assets from scripts and automated CI/CD actions.
It is the web-based visual interface for working on projects by hand, not for pipeline automation.

options.text: The Foundry Toolkit extension for Visual Studio Code
options.why: It simplifies a developer's work inside the editor; it is not run by a DevOps pipeline.
It is a central MCP-based knowledge connection for agents, not a way to manage assets.

cards.question: How do a Microsoft Foundry **project** and a Microsoft Foundry **resource** relate, and what does each provide?
cards.answer:
- **Project** — holds the solution's resource connections, data, code and other elements
- **Resource** — the Azure resource that provides compute, data storage, AI tools and other services
- Each project belongs to **one** resource; a resource has one or more projects, one of them the **default project**
cards.explanation: The split keeps project-specific assets apart from the shared cloud services. That gives the right level of centralization with a minimum of administrative resource management, which suits the most common task: building generative AI chat apps and agents. You can build without Foundry by provisioning individual AI resources, but Foundry is recommended for all but the simplest solutions. Older *classic* Foundry projects may use a **hub-based** architecture instead.
cards.addition: Current docs list the classic resource model as a hub plus separate Azure OpenAI and Azure AI Services resources, replaced by a single Foundry resource with projects. Hub-based projects stay accessible in the Foundry (classic) portal.

cards.question: Name the **four** kinds of assets developers manage in a Microsoft Foundry project.
cards.answer:
- **Models** — LLM deployments based on the **Foundry Models** catalog
- **Agents** — named configurations of an LLM, instructions and tools
- **Tools** — built-in functions, MCP connections and Foundry Tools that agents use
- **Knowledge** — knowledge stores whose data agents use to contextualize prompts
cards.explanation: The four build on each other: a model deployment is the base, an agent wraps a model with instructions and tools, and agents reach knowledge stores through tools. Foundry Models is a catalog of models from Microsoft, OpenAI and other providers. All four assets live in the project, while compute, storage and the Foundry Tools come from the parent Foundry resource.

explanation_images.alt: A Microsoft Foundry project inside a Microsoft Foundry resource, with four asset groups: Models, Agents, Tools and Knowledge

cards.question: Through which **two endpoints** can a client app reach the LLMs deployed in a Microsoft Foundry project, and which APIs does each expect?
cards.answer:
- **Project endpoint** — Foundry-specific APIs and SDKs
- **Azure OpenAI endpoint** — OpenAI APIs and SDKs
cards.explanation: Both endpoints reach the same model deployments; the choice follows the SDK the app is written with. An app built on the OpenAI SDKs uses OpenAI syntax and connects to the Azure OpenAI endpoint; code using the Foundry SDK goes to the project endpoint. The project endpoint is also the way to agents, which are built and consumed through the Foundry Agent Service. In the Foundry portal you find the endpoints and keys that client apps need.
cards.addition: Current docs describe the new model as one unified project client (`azure-ai-projects` 2.x) plus `OpenAI()` against **one project endpoint**, replacing several packages such as `AzureOpenAI()` against five or more endpoints.

cards.question: What does an **agent** in Microsoft Foundry encapsulate, and which service do you develop and consume it with?
cards.answer:
- A named AI configuration of an **LLM**, **instructions** and **tools**
- Developed and consumed with the **Microsoft Foundry Agent Service**, through the **project endpoint**
cards.explanation: Together the three parts define an autonomous AI entity that can automate tasks and collaborate with users and with other agents. Note the contrast to plain models: a model deployment is reachable through the project endpoint or the Azure OpenAI endpoint, but the Agent Service, and with it every agent, sits behind the project endpoint.
cards.addition: Current docs call an agent defined declaratively (instructions, model, tools) and hosted by Foundry a **prompt agent**; your own containerized code that Foundry runs is a **hosted agent**.

cards.question: The **Tools** assets of a Microsoft Foundry project come from **three** sources. Name them.
cards.answer:
- **Built-in tools** — e.g. web search, code interpreter
- **MCP connections** — custom and third-party tools via Model Context Protocol
- **Foundry Tools** — prebuilt AI services such as text analysis, speech, translation and content understanding
cards.explanation: Agents use tools based on built-in functionality, or on MCP connections to tools that you or third parties provide. Foundry Tools differ from both: a suite of AI services for common tasks that you can use in your Foundry-based solutions, hosted in the Foundry resource associated with your projects rather than in a project itself. Agents also use tools to connect to knowledge stores.

cards.question: Agents in your Microsoft Foundry project must ground prompts in data from several knowledge sources, and you want to integrate them through **one central connection**. What do you use?
cards.answer: **Foundry IQ**, which creates a single, central MCP-based knowledge connection in the project.
cards.explanation: Agents use tools to connect to knowledge stores and use their data to contextualize prompts. With many stores, each would need its own connection; Foundry IQ simplifies integration by giving the project one MCP-based knowledge connection. In the Foundry portal you create Foundry IQ knowledge sources next to MCP connections to tools.
cards.addition: Foundry IQ builds a multi-source **knowledge base** of knowledge sources and queries it with agentic retrieval; **Azure AI Search** provides the underlying indexing and retrieval infrastructure.

options.why: It creates one central MCP-based knowledge connection over multiple sources.
They are prebuilt AI services such as speech and translation, not a knowledge connection.
It is the catalog the project's LLM deployments are based on.
It is the service for developing and consuming agents, not the way to integrate knowledge sources.

cards.question: What are **Foundry Tools** in Microsoft Foundry, what do they gain you over a solution built on generative AI agents alone, and under which **two** older names do they still appear in some APIs and SDKs?
cards.answer:
- **Foundry Tools** — a set of out-of-the-box **prebuilt APIs and models** for common AI tasks
- Gain: a **more cost-effective and predictable** solution
- Older names: **Azure AI Services**, before that **Azure Cognitive Services**
cards.explanation: Generative models and agents are the focus of most AI projects, but many tasks are common enough that ready-made functionality covers them: analysing text, converting speech, translating, extracting fields from forms. Integrating that functionality is cheaper and behaves more predictably than leaving the task to an agent. The old names are still reflected in some APIs and SDKs, so expect them in code.

cards.question: Name the **five** Foundry Tools in Microsoft Foundry and what each one does.
cards.answer:
- **Azure Language** — text analysis (entities, sentiment, summarization), conversational language models, question answering
- **Azure Speech** — text to speech, speech to text, real-time live speech
- **Azure Translator** — text translation between many languages
- **Azure Document Intelligence** — prebuilt or custom models extract fields from invoices, receipts, forms
- **Azure Content Understanding** — multimodal data extraction from documents, images, video, audio
cards.explanation: Sort them by input. Language and Translator work on text; Speech converts between audio and text, including live speech for conversational apps and agents. Document Intelligence and Content Understanding both extract data from forms, so they are the pair to tell apart: Document Intelligence covers complex documents such as invoices and receipts, while Content Understanding is multimodal and also reads images, videos and audio streams.

cards.question: An insurer wants to build models that extract data from claim forms **and** from damage photos, video recordings and recorded phone calls, all with one Foundry Tool in Microsoft Foundry. Which tool fits?
cards.answer: **Azure Content Understanding** — multimodal content analysis across documents, images, video and audio.
cards.explanation: The deciding requirement is the mix of input types. Document Intelligence also extracts fields from forms, invoices and receipts, so it would cover the claim forms, but not the photos, videos or calls. Content Understanding is the one Foundry Tool built for multimodal content: it lets you build models that extract data from forms and documents, images, videos and audio streams.

options.why: It provides multimodal analysis to extract data from forms and documents, images, videos and audio streams.
It extracts fields from complex documents such as invoices, receipts and forms, but not from photos, video or audio.
It analyses natural language text, for example entities, sentiment and summaries, not images, video or audio.
It converts speech to text and text to speech, but does not extract data from forms, photos or video.

cards.question: A client application must call Azure Translator, a Foundry Tool hosted in your Microsoft Foundry resource. Which endpoint does it connect to, and which **two** ways can it authenticate?
cards.answer:
- Endpoint: the **tool-specific endpoint** in the Microsoft Foundry resource
- Authenticate with the project **authentication key** or with **token-based authentication**
- Then call the tool-specific **APIs and SDKs**
cards.explanation: Foundry Tools live in the Foundry resource, so each tool is reached through its own endpoint on that resource. Some tools also have a user interface in the Foundry portal for configuring and testing them before you write code. You can still provision some tools as individual Azure resources outside a Foundry resource, but new projects should use the tools in a Foundry resource.
cards.addition: Token-based authentication with Microsoft Entra ID only works on the resource's **custom subdomain** endpoint, not on regional endpoints, and the caller needs an RBAC role such as **Cognitive Services User**. A key travels in the `Ocp-Apim-Subscription-Key` header; a token as `Authorization: Bearer`.

cards.question: Name the **three** kinds of APIs and SDKs you plan to use when building AI solutions on Azure with Microsoft Foundry, and what each one is for.
cards.answer:
- **Microsoft Foundry SDK** — connect to Foundry **projects** and Foundry-specific assets such as **agents** and **Foundry IQ** knowledge stores
- **OpenAI API** — use **OpenAI SDKs** to build chat apps on Foundry models that support OpenAI syntax
- **Foundry Tools SDKs** — service-specific libraries to consume Foundry Tools; the tools also have **REST APIs**
cards.explanation: The split follows what you talk to. Project assets that only exist in Foundry, like agents and Foundry IQ knowledge, need the Foundry SDK. A plain chat app on a model that speaks OpenAI syntax can use the familiar OpenAI SDKs. Prebuilt services such as Language or Speech come with their own per-service libraries, or you call their REST endpoints directly. You can write all of this in C#, Python, Node, TypeScript, Java and other languages.
cards.addition: In Python, the Foundry SDK is the `azure-ai-projects` package. You create an `AIProjectClient` with the project endpoint `https://<resource-name>.services.ai.azure.com/api/projects/<project-name>`, and `project.get_openai_client()` returns an OpenAI client.

cards.question: A Python app must connect to a Microsoft Foundry project, use the project's **agents** and query a **Foundry IQ** knowledge store. Which SDK fits?
cards.answer: The **Microsoft Foundry SDK**.
cards.explanation: Agents and Foundry IQ knowledge stores are Foundry-specific assets of a project, and the Foundry SDK is the library made to reach them. The OpenAI SDKs only cover chat on models that support OpenAI syntax. Foundry Tools SDKs target single prebuilt services. The Foundry Toolkit is an editor extension, not a library your app calls.

options.why: It connects code to Foundry projects and Foundry-specific assets such as agents and Foundry IQ knowledge stores.

options.text: OpenAI SDK through the OpenAI API
options.why: It builds chat applications on Foundry models that support OpenAI syntax, not access to Foundry-specific project assets.
They are service-specific libraries for prebuilt Foundry Tools such as Language or Speech, not for agents or Foundry IQ.

options.text: Foundry Toolkit for Visual Studio Code
options.why: It is a VS Code extension that helps the developer manage and test resources; the app itself does not call it.

cards.question: Name the **five** tasks the **Foundry Toolkit extension for Visual Studio Code** simplifies when you build Microsoft Foundry generative AI apps.
cards.answer:
- **Browse and manage project resources** — deployed models, agents, connections, vector stores
- **Deploy models** from the model catalog
- **Test models and agents** in integrated playgrounds
- **Configure declarative and hosted agents** with a visual designer and YAML files
- **Generate integration code** to connect agents to your apps
cards.explanation: The Microsoft Foundry portal handles many development tasks, but developers also need to write, test and deploy code. The toolkit brings the project into Visual Studio Code: you deploy a model from the catalog, try it or an agent in a playground, define the agent visually or in YAML, and then generate the code that connects it to your app, all in one editor.

explanation_images.alt: Foundry Toolkit in VS Code: a Resources tree with Models, Prompt Agents, Workflows, Hosted Agents, Tools and Knowledge, and a Tools list with Model Catalog, Model Playground, Remote and Local Agent Playgrounds and Deploy Hosted Agents.

cards.question: Which **four** developer tools, two editors and two GitHub offerings, suit building AI apps on Azure, and what is each one for?
cards.answer:
- **Visual Studio** — an **IDE**, suits .NET developers building Windows apps
- **Visual Studio Code** — a **code editor**, suits web developers using many open-source languages and libraries
- **GitHub** — source control and DevOps management
- **GitHub Copilot** — AI assistant for developer productivity
cards.explanation: Both editors are suitable for AI apps on Azure. Pick the one that supports the languages, SDKs and APIs you need and that you are most comfortable with. Visual Studio and VS Code both integrate natively with GitHub, which makes it a central part of team development, and both give access to GitHub Copilot inside the editor.

cards.question: Your team already builds chat apps with the **OpenAI SDKs**. A new chat app must run on a Microsoft Foundry model that supports OpenAI syntax, and the team wants to keep its SDKs. Which API do you plan to use?
cards.answer: The **OpenAI API**, called through the OpenAI SDKs.
cards.explanation: The OpenAI API lets OpenAI SDKs talk to Foundry models that support OpenAI syntax, so a plain chat app needs no Foundry-specific library. The Microsoft Foundry SDK only becomes necessary when the code must reach Foundry-specific project assets, such as agents or Foundry IQ knowledge stores. Foundry Tools SDKs serve the prebuilt AI services, not chat models.
cards.addition: Current docs recommend the OpenAI SDK for maximum OpenAI compatibility, lowest latency and embeddings, against `https://<resource-name>.openai.azure.com/openai/v1`. They recommend the Foundry SDK for agents, evaluations and other Foundry-specific features.

cards.question: Name the **six** principles for responsible AI that Microsoft has adopted.
cards.answer:
- **Fairness** — treat all people fairly, without bias
- **Reliability and safety** — perform reliably and safely
- **Privacy and security** — be secure and respect privacy
- **Inclusiveness** — empower everyone and engage people
- **Transparency** — be understandable
- **Accountability** — people are accountable for AI systems
cards.explanation: AI needs these more than ordinary software: its decisions come from probabilistic models that depend on their training data, and its human-like nature makes users trust it a great deal. The principles differ in focus. Fairness is about unbiased predictions for groups; inclusiveness about benefits for all of society and diverse input into design. Privacy protects the data itself; transparency tells users how the system and their data are used. Accountability keeps the responsibility with people, not the system.

cards.question: A bank's loan approval model must not give applicants an advantage or disadvantage because of their gender or ethnicity. Which Microsoft **responsible AI principle** does this requirement address?
cards.answer: **Fairness**.
cards.explanation: The loan approval model is the standard example for fairness: its predictions must not incorporate bias based on gender, ethnicity or other factors that favour or penalise specific groups of applicants. Inclusiveness names the same factors, but asks something else: that AI brings benefits to all parts of society and that diverse people shape its design. The bias of individual predictions is a fairness question.

options.why: Fairness requires that predictions do not favour or penalise groups of people, such as loan applicants of a certain gender or ethnicity.
Inclusiveness is about AI benefiting and engaging all parts of society, not about bias in a model's predictions.
Transparency makes users aware of how the system works and its limits; it does not itself remove bias.
Accountability assigns responsibility for the system to its developers within a governance framework; it does not define what an unbiased prediction is.

cards.question: Tools exist to evaluate, quantify and mitigate unfairness in machine learning models. According to Microsoft's responsible AI guidance, what must a team do **beyond** such tooling to ensure fairness?
cards.answer:
Consider fairness **from the beginning** of development:
- **Review the training data** so it represents all potentially affected subjects
- **Evaluate predictive performance for subsections** of the user population throughout the lifecycle
cards.explanation: Fairness of machine-learned systems is still an active research area, and tooling alone isn't sufficient. A model learns from its data, so training data must represent everyone the system may affect. Measuring predictive performance per subsection of the users, not only overall, shows when one group is served worse. Fairness is considered from the start, and that per-group evaluation continues throughout the development lifecycle, not once at the end.

cards.question: You build an AI model that diagnoses patient symptoms and recommends prescriptions. Which **two** practices does Microsoft's **reliability and safety** principle call for?
cards.answer:
- **Rigorous testing and deployment management** so the system works as expected before release
- Appropriate **thresholds** when evaluating the **confidence scores** of predictions
cards.explanation: In systems like medical diagnosis or autonomous vehicles, unreliability can put human life at risk. AI applications are software, so they need the same rigorous testing and deployment processes as any other software. On top of that, machine learning models are probabilistic: each prediction comes with a confidence score, and engineers have to set sensible thresholds for how confident a prediction must be.

cards.question: Under Microsoft's **privacy and security** principle for AI, at which **two** stages can data raise privacy or security concerns, and what is required?
cards.answer:
- **Training**: large volumes of data that may contain personal details
- **Production**: new data the system uses to make predictions or take action
- Required: **safeguards** that protect data and customer content
cards.explanation: The principle says AI systems should be secure and respect privacy. The concern does not end once a model is trained. A system in production keeps receiving new data, and that data can be just as sensitive as the training data. Protection therefore has to cover both the data the model learned from and the data it processes later.

cards.question: Which practice does Microsoft recommend to optimise an AI application for **inclusiveness**?
cards.answer: Include input from **as diverse a group of people as possible** in the **design, development and testing** of the application.
cards.explanation: Inclusiveness means AI systems should empower everyone and engage people: AI should bring benefits to all parts of society, regardless of physical ability, gender, sexual orientation, ethnicity or other factors. Do not confuse it with fairness. Fairness checks that a model's predictions do not favour or penalise groups, as in loan approval. Inclusiveness asks whom the system serves and who shapes it, which is why diverse people take part at every stage, not only in a final check.

cards.question: Under Microsoft's **transparency** principle, what should users of an AI system based on a machine learning model be made aware of?
cards.answer:
- The system's **purpose**, how it works and its **limitations**
- **Factors affecting accuracy**, such as the number of training cases and the most influential features
- The **confidence score** of predictions
- With personal data: how it is **used and retained**, and **who has access**
cards.explanation: Transparency means AI systems should be understandable. The disclosures work on two levels. For the system as a whole, users learn what it is for and what it cannot do. For each prediction, the confidence score shows how sure the model is. Training-set size and influential features are examples of what limits accuracy. Telling users how personal data is handled is also transparency; actually protecting that data is privacy and security.

cards.question: A facial recognition system takes images of people to recognise them. You must **tell users** how their images are used, how long they are retained and who has access to them. Under which Microsoft responsible AI principle does this disclosure fall?
cards.answer: **Transparency**.
cards.explanation: Making it clear to users how their personal data is used and retained, and who has access to it, is part of transparency: users should understand the system they deal with. Privacy and security is the neighbouring principle. It requires safeguards that actually protect the data. Telling users about the data handling is transparency; protecting the data is privacy and security.

options.why: Transparency requires making clear to users how their personal data is used and retained and who has access to it.
Privacy and security calls for safeguards that protect the data; informing users about its use is transparency.
Accountability puts responsibility for the system on its developers within a governance framework; it is not about informing users.
Fairness is about predictions not favouring or penalising groups of people.

cards.question: Many AI systems seem to operate autonomously. Under Microsoft's **accountability** principle, who is responsible for the system meeting responsibility requirements, and within what?
cards.answer:
- The **developers** who trained and validated the models and defined the logic that bases decisions on their predictions
- Working within a **framework of governance and organizational principles** with clearly defined responsible and legal standards
cards.explanation: Accountability means people are accountable for AI systems. An apparently autonomous system does not take over that responsibility: the decisions follow from models people trained and validated, and from decision logic people defined. The governance framework makes the standards explicit, so designers and developers know which responsible and legal requirements the solution has to meet.

cards.question: Put the steps in order to get from signing in to a first chat with a deployed model in the **Microsoft Foundry portal**.
cards.answer: **New Foundry** on → create project → model card in **Discover > Models** → **Deploy** → **Instructions** in the playground → chat.
cards.explanation: A **project** organizes the models, resources and data of an AI solution, so it comes before any model. The **model card** describes a model's capabilities and limitations, so you can judge whether it suits your requirements before deploying it. Only a **deployment** lets you work with the model in your project; when it is ready, the model playground opens on its own. In the **Instructions** box you tell the model what role to play, here an assistant that gives advice on AI software development.
items: Sign in at https://ai.azure.com and enable the New Foundry option in the top toolbar
Create a project; under Advanced options set the Foundry resource, subscription, resource group and region
On the Discover page, open the Models tab, search the model and open its model card
Select Deploy with the default settings
In the model playground, enter the system instructions in the Instructions box
Send a query in the chat window and read the response

cards.question: A client app must connect to your Microsoft Foundry project. Where in the **Foundry portal** do you find the project's **key and endpoints**, where the **parent Foundry resource's** endpoint, and what is each one for?
cards.answer:
- **Home** (project home page) → the **key** (key-based authentication), the **project endpoint** (Responses API, Foundry APIs such as the Agent service) and the **Azure OpenAI endpoint** (OpenAI APIs: Chat Completions, Responses)
- **Manage** (management center) → **Parent resource** → the **Foundry resource endpoint** (resource-level features, e.g. Foundry Tools shared by all projects)
cards.explanation: The management center, where you view and administer projects and their parent resources, splits a *resource* level from a *project* level. The resource is the Foundry resource in Azure: it holds the connections to Foundry services and models and controls user access centrally. One resource can support several projects; the first one created is its **default project**. Both project endpoints offer the Responses API: take the project endpoint for Foundry-specific APIs, the OpenAI endpoint for Chat Completions. In most production scenarios, consider Microsoft Entra ID instead of the key.

explanation_images.alt: Foundry project home page with the fields API key, Project endpoint and Azure OpenAI endpoint, each with a copy button
Foundry portal Manage page: Resource details and Project details in the left pane, the project marked Default project, with Project endpoint and a Parent resource link

cards.question: You want to test a model deployed in your Microsoft Foundry project **from inside Visual Studio Code**. Put the steps in order.
cards.answer: Install **Foundry Toolkit for VS Code** → open its page → set the **default project** → view the deployment under **Models** → **Developer Tools > Build > Model playground**.
cards.explanation: Developers spend much of their time in VS Code, and the Foundry Toolkit lets them work with Foundry project resources without leaving it. The pane only shows your project after you connect to Azure and pick it as the default project under **Microsoft Foundry Resources**. Expanding the project and then **Models** shows each deployment's details. The model playground then opens an interactive test chat in VS Code, like the playground in the Foundry portal.

explanation_images.alt: Foundry Toolkit pane in Visual Studio Code with the resources section (including the Foundry project) and Developer Tools with Discover, Build and Monitor

items: On the Extensions page, search for Foundry Toolkit and install Foundry Toolkit for VS Code
Open the Foundry Toolkit page in the left navigation bar
Under Microsoft Foundry Resources, sign in to Azure and set your Foundry project as the default project
Expand the project, then Models, and select the deployment to view its details
Under Developer Tools, expand Build, select Model playground and pick the model

cards.question: Which web portal should you use to work with assets in a Microsoft Foundry project?
cards.answer: **The Microsoft Foundry portal**.
cards.explanation: The Foundry portal is the web-based visual interface for Foundry projects. Most AI development starts there: you find, compare, deploy and test models, create and test agents, create MCP connections to tools and Foundry IQ knowledge sources, manage resource configuration and user access, and look up endpoints and keys. To automate the same project operations in scripts or CI/CD pipelines, you use the Microsoft Foundry SDK instead.

options.why: Unit 1.1.3 names the Foundry portal, not the Azure portal, as the interface for developing and managing Foundry projects and their assets.
Microsoft Copilot is not a portal for project assets; the module never names it as a Foundry development tool.
Unit 1.1.3: the Microsoft Foundry portal is the web-based visual interface for working with AI projects and their models, agents, tools and knowledge connections.

cards.question: Which component of Microsoft Foundry provides pre-built services for common AI tasks?
cards.answer: **Foundry Tools**.
cards.explanation: Foundry Tools are out-of-the-box prebuilt APIs and models: Azure Language, Speech, Translator, Document Intelligence and Content Understanding. They are hosted in the Foundry resource and often give a more cost-effective and predictable solution than generative AI agents alone. Foundry Models, by contrast, is the model catalog you deploy LLMs from, and Foundry IQ is the central knowledge connection for agents. Foundry Tools were formerly called Azure AI Services, and before that Azure Cognitive Services.

options.why: Unit 1.1.4: Foundry Tools are a set of out-of-the-box prebuilt APIs and models for common AI tasks such as text analysis, speech, translation and document extraction.
Unit 1.1.3: Foundry Models is the catalog of models from Microsoft, OpenAI and other providers that you deploy as LLMs, not a set of prebuilt task services.
Unit 1.1.3: Foundry IQ creates a single, central MCP-based connection to knowledge sources for agents, not prebuilt AI services.

cards.question: Which extension should you use in Visual Studio Code to work with Foundry projects?
cards.answer: **Foundry Toolkit for Visual Studio Code**.
cards.explanation: The Foundry Toolkit simplifies the Foundry workflow inside VS Code: browse and manage project resources (deployed models, agents, connections, vector stores), deploy models from the catalog, test models and agents in integrated playgrounds, configure declarative and hosted agents with a visual designer and YAML files, and generate integration code. GitHub Copilot is an AI assistant that improves developer productivity; it does not manage Foundry project resources.

options.text: Python extension for Visual Studio Code
options.why: It is not a Foundry tool; unit 1.1.5 does not mention it and names the Foundry Toolkit as the extension for working with Foundry projects.
Unit 1.1.5: GitHub Copilot is an AI assistant that improves developer productivity, not a tool for managing Foundry project resources.

options.text: Foundry Toolkit for Visual Studio Code
options.why: Unit 1.1.5: the Foundry Toolkit extension lets you browse and manage project resources, deploy and test models and agents, and generate integration code.

cards.question: Name the **two** broad categories of models in the **Microsoft Foundry** model catalog, and how each one is billed.
cards.answer:
- **Foundry Models sold directly by Azure** — billed through your Azure subscription; Azure OpenAI models plus models from Microsoft and other providers
- **Foundry Models from partners and community** — from trusted partners and the community, each with its own licensing and pricing
cards.explanation: The split decides how you pay and what you sign before deploying. A company that wants every model on its Azure bill picks from the first category. Partner and community models usually need an Azure Marketplace subscription: at deployment you review their terms of use and select Agree and Proceed. Models sold directly by Azure, such as the Azure OpenAI model GPT-4o-mini, need no Marketplace subscription.
cards.addition: Models sold by Azure are also hosted and operated by Azure as part of the Foundry Models service, covered by Azure service-level agreements, and supported by Microsoft.

cards.question: In the **Microsoft Foundry** model catalog, what shows a single model's provider, capabilities, benchmark metrics, responsible AI considerations and deployment options?
cards.answer: Its **model card**.
cards.explanation: Every model in the catalog has a model card that gathers its key information in one place. You open it after searching or filtering the catalog. It is also where you start a deployment and review the supported deployment types, and its Benchmarks tab shows how this one model compares with similar models.

cards.question: Your app receives product photos and must answer questions about what each photo shows. Which model from the **Microsoft Foundry** catalog fits?
cards.answer: **GPT-4.1**, an image analysis model with multimodal input.
cards.explanation: Image analysis models accept text and images in one prompt and answer in natural language. The trap is the name: image generation models create pictures from text, they do not read them.

options.why: It accepts multimodal input (text and images) and generates natural language output about the image.
It is an image generation model: it creates images from text descriptions.
It is a video generation model: it creates video from text descriptions.
It converts text into numerical vectors for semantic search; it does not analyse images.

cards.question: Your app analyses **legal documents** and needs the best accuracy in that domain. What kind of model should you look for in the **Microsoft Foundry** catalog, and which filter finds it?
cards.answer: A **regional or domain-specific model**, found with the **Industry** filter.
cards.explanation: Some catalog models are optimized for one language, region or industry, for example models trained on medical literature, legal documents or specific language corpora. In their own domain they often outperform general-purpose models. Use them when specialized performance in one domain or language matters more than broad general ability.

cards.question: Besides keyword search, name the **six** attributes you can filter the **Microsoft Foundry** model catalog by.
cards.answer:
- **Collection** — organized sets, e.g. provided directly in Azure, Hugging Face repository
- **Capabilities** — abilities: **reasoning**, **tool calling**, **multimodal processing**
- **Source** — the provider, e.g. Azure OpenAI, Cohere, Mistral, Meta
- **Inference tasks** — jobs such as summarization or translation
- **Fine-tuning methods** — supported fine-tuning techniques
- **Industry** — models trained on industry-specific data
cards.explanation: Two pairs get confused. Collection says which set a model belongs to; Source says who built it. Capabilities says what a model can do: reasoning is complex problem-solving, tool calling is API and function integration, multimodal processing handles text, images and audio. Inference tasks says which job you want done, such as text generation, image generation or speech synthesis. Industry models often beat general-purpose models in their own domain.

explanation_images.alt: Foundry portal model catalog with the filter list Collections, Capabilities, Source, Inference tasks, Fine-tuning methods and Industry on the left

cards.question: Name the **four** kinds of language model in the **Microsoft Foundry** catalog: two told apart by size, two by purpose.
cards.answer:
- **Large language model (LLM)** — deep reasoning, complex generation, extensive context understanding; needs more compute
- **Small language model (SLM)** — fast and cheap for common NLP tasks; runs on edge devices
- **Chat completion model** — coherent text for chat and content generation
- **Reasoning model** — breaks down complex problems and shows its reasoning
cards.explanation: LLMs: GPT-5, Mistral Large, Llama 3 70B. SLMs: Phi-4, Mistral OSS models, Llama 3 8B; pick one when speed and cost matter more than the hardest reasoning, or the model must run on lower-end hardware. Most catalog language models are chat completion models, powering conversational interfaces. Reasoning models such as Claude Opus 4.6 do better in mathematics, coding, science, strategy and logistics.

cards.question: Name the **six** types of task-specific (specialized) models in the **Microsoft Foundry** model catalog, each with its example model.
cards.answer:
- **Embedding** — text into numbers for semantic search, RAG (text-embedding-3-large)
- **Image generation** — images from text (GPT-image-1)
- **Video generation** — video from text (Sora 2)
- **Image analysis** — text and image input, text output (GPT-4.1)
- **Text to speech** — synthesized speech from text (GPT-4o-tts)
- **Speech to text** — transcripts from speech audio (GPT-4o-transcribe)
cards.explanation: Embeddings let an app find information by meaning rather than exact keywords, which drives semantic search, recommendation systems and RAG; text-embedding-3-small and Cohere's models are further options. Two traps: image analysis reads images, image generation creates them, for marketing materials, illustrations or design mockups. Text to speech and speech to text are opposite directions: check whether the audio is the input or the output.

cards.question: A field app must run a language model **on an edge device** with modest hardware. It handles common NLP tasks, and speed and cost matter more than the hardest reasoning. Which kind of model from the **Microsoft Foundry** catalog fits?
cards.answer: A **small language model (SLM)**, such as Phi-4 or Llama 3 8B.
cards.explanation: SLMs give up the deepest reasoning in exchange for efficiency and cost-effectiveness, and they can run on lower-end hardware or edge devices. LLMs such as GPT-5 or Llama 3 70B handle deep reasoning, complex content generation and extensive context understanding, but they require more computational resources. Choose the LLM for sophisticated applications that need that depth; choose the SLM when speed, cost or hardware set the limit.

options.why: It offers efficiency and cost-effectiveness for common NLP tasks and can run on lower-end hardware or edge devices.
It is built for deep reasoning and complex content generation and requires more computational resources.
It targets complex problems in mathematics, coding, science, strategy and logistics, not fast, cheap common tasks.
It converts text into numerical representations for semantic search; it does not generate text responses.

cards.question: Name the **two** places in the Microsoft Foundry portal where you explore model benchmarks, and what each one shows.
cards.answer:
- **Model leaderboard** — in the model catalog; ranks all models by quality, safety, estimated cost and throughput
- **Benchmarks tab** — on one model's model card; that model across metrics and datasets, with charts against similar models
cards.explanation: The two views work as a funnel. The leaderboard is the cross-model view: it helps you spot the top performers for a metric or scenario across the whole catalog. Once you have candidates, open one model's card and its Benchmarks tab to look closer at that single model. Both give objective, measurable data, so you can compare models before you deploy anything.

explanation_images.alt: Model leaderboard page under Discover in the Foundry portal, with bar charts for Quality (quality index, higher is better), Safety (attack success rate, lower is better), Throughput and Estimated cost

cards.question: Into which **four** categories does the Microsoft Foundry portal organize model benchmarks, and what does each measure?
cards.answer:
- **Quality** — accurate, coherent, contextually appropriate responses
- **Safety** — resisting harmful, biased or inappropriate output
- **Cost** — token pricing of the model
- **Performance** — how quickly and efficiently it responds
cards.explanation: The categories mirror the Model leaderboard, which ranks models by quality, safety, estimated cost and throughput. Choosing a model means weighing them against each other: a slightly less accurate model that is much faster or cheaper can serve an app better than the top quality scorer. Safety weighs most in customer-facing apps; for batch jobs, cost can matter more than speed.

cards.question: Microsoft Foundry's quality benchmarks use **eight** public datasets. Name them with what each measures, and say what the **Quality index** does with them.
cards.answer:
- **Quality index** — average accuracy across these datasets, 0 to 1, higher is better
- **Arena-Hard** — adversarial question answering
- **BIG-Bench Hard** — reasoning capabilities
- **GPQA** — graduate-level multi-discipline questions
- **HumanEval+** and **MBPP+** — code generation
- **MATH** — mathematical reasoning
- **MMLU-Pro** — general knowledge
- **IFEval** — instruction following
cards.explanation: The datasets span reasoning, knowledge, question answering, math and coding, so the Quality index is one high-level number for general-purpose language tasks. Public datasets and standardized methods keep scores comparable across models. Keep two pairs apart: BIG-Bench Hard is reasoning in general, MATH is mathematical reasoning; MMLU-Pro is general knowledge, GPQA is graduate level. When your app maps to one task, a scenario leaderboard is the better starting point.
cards.addition: The current docs list a different Quality index set: BIG-Bench Hard, ChemBench, FrontierScience, GPQA, MBPP+, MMLU-Pro, MuSR and tau2 telecom. Arena-Hard and MATH now appear only in scenario leaderboards; HumanEval+ and IFEval are in neither list.

cards.question: Name the **three** safety dimensions Microsoft Foundry's model benchmarks evaluate, with the benchmark and score behind each.
cards.answer:
- **Harmful behavior detection** — **HarmBench**, scored as **Attack Success Rate (ASR)**; lower is safer
- **Toxic content detection** — **ToxiGen**, **F1 score**; higher detects hate speech better
- **Sensitive domain knowledge** — **WMDP** (Weapons of Mass Destruction Proxy); higher means more knowledge of dangerous capabilities
cards.explanation: HarmBench measures how well a model resists generating unsafe content. ToxiGen measures how well it identifies adversarial and implicit hate speech across references to minority groups. WMDP measures knowledge in biosecurity, cybersecurity and chemical security. Mind the directions: for ASR low is good, for ToxiGen high is good. Safety scores matter most for customer-facing apps and regulated industries, where harmful output is a serious risk.
cards.addition: Microsoft's benchmark documentation states it outright: a higher WMDP accuracy is worse behavior from a safety standpoint.

cards.question: Which **three** functional areas does the **HarmBench** benchmark test in Microsoft Foundry's safety benchmarks?
cards.answer:
- **Standard harmful behaviors** — cybercrime, illegal activities, general harm
- **Contextually harmful behaviors** — misinformation, harassment, bullying
- **Copyright violations** — reproducing copyrighted material
cards.explanation: Together they show how well a model resists generating unsafe content, expressed as an Attack Success Rate where lower is safer. The first area is plainly harmful requests; the second is harm that depends on context, such as false claims or attacks on a person; the third is reproducing protected text. Such scores matter most for customer-facing applications, where harmful output poses significant concerns.

cards.question: You compare models in the Microsoft Foundry model benchmarks. Which **three** of these values are better when they are **lower**?
cards.answer: **Attack Success Rate (ASR)**, **Estimated cost** and **mean time to first token**.
cards.explanation: Each of the three counts something you want little of: successful attempts to get unsafe content, money, and waiting time. Values that measure skill or output go the other way. The Quality index and the ToxiGen F1 score are better when higher, and so is mean generated tokens per second, the leaderboard's throughput summary. Mixing up the directions turns a ranking upside down.

options.why: A lower ASR means a safer, more robust model.
Lower estimated cost means a more cost-effective model.
It is the leaderboard's latency summary; lower means the first token arrives sooner.
It is an average accuracy from 0 to 1, where higher means stronger overall performance.
A higher F1 score means better detection of adversarial and implicit hate speech.

cards.question: Name the **three** cost benchmarks Microsoft Foundry shows for serverless API deployments and Azure OpenAI models.
cards.answer:
- **Cost per input tokens** — price per 1 million tokens you send
- **Cost per output tokens** — price per 1 million tokens the model generates
- **Estimated cost** — both combined at a **3:1** input-to-output ratio into one number; lower is better
cards.explanation: Input and output tokens are priced separately, which makes two models hard to compare at a glance. Estimated cost assumes three input tokens for every output token and merges both prices into a single comparable figure. Cost benchmarks help you find a model that delivers the quality you need at a price that fits your usage patterns and budget.
cards.addition: Current docs also describe a newer cost benchmark: the actual USD cost of running each model on the quality benchmark datasets, using real input, reasoning and output token counts instead of a fixed token ratio.

cards.question: Which group of Microsoft Foundry performance benchmarks measures how long a request takes, and which **six** measurements does it include?
cards.answer:
**Latency**:
- **Latency mean** — average seconds per request
- **Latency P50** — median; 50 % of requests finish faster
- **Latency P90** — 90 % finish faster
- **Latency P95** — 95 % finish faster
- **Latency P99** — 99 % finish faster
- **Time to first token (TTFT)** — wait until the first token arrives when streaming
cards.explanation: The mean is one average; the percentiles describe the spread. A P95 of 2 seconds means 95 % of requests complete faster than 2 seconds. For a streaming chat app, TTFT is how long the user waits before text appears. The leaderboard summarizes latency as mean TTFT, where lower is better. Latency matters for real-time applications, where the user experience depends on responsiveness.

cards.question: Which group of Microsoft Foundry performance benchmarks measures how fast tokens flow, and which **three** measurements does it include?
cards.answer:
**Throughput**:
- **Generated tokens per second (GTPS)** — output tokens only
- **Total tokens per second (TTPS)** — input and output tokens combined
- **Time between tokens** — interval between consecutive tokens
cards.explanation: GTPS and TTPS differ only in what they count: GTPS the tokens the model produces, TTPS everything processed. The leaderboard summarizes throughput as mean GTPS, where higher is better. Time between tokens is a time but sits under throughput; time to first token is latency. High-throughput, low-latency models give better experiences in interactive apps; for batch jobs, cost can take priority.

cards.question: Besides sorting by one metric, which **three** features does the Microsoft Foundry model leaderboard offer to find the model that fits your requirements?
cards.answer:
- **Scenario leaderboards** — rankings for one use case: reasoning, coding, math, question answering, groundedness
- **Trade-off charts** — two metrics at once: quality against cost, throughput or safety
- **Side-by-side comparison** — two or three selected models compared in detail
cards.explanation: Each answers a different question. Scenario leaderboards: which model is best at my task, instead of the overall Quality index. Trade-off charts: which model balances two needs; models near the top-right corner do well on both, and a slightly less accurate model that is much faster or cheaper may serve you better. Side-by-side comparison: how my shortlisted models differ in detail.

cards.question: Your app mainly solves **math** problems. Which Microsoft Foundry leaderboard view should you start from to shortlist models?
cards.answer: The **math scenario leaderboard**.
cards.explanation: The overall Quality index averages accuracy across reasoning, knowledge, question answering, math and coding, so it mixes your task with many others. When your app maps to a particular scenario, start with that scenario leaderboard rather than relying solely on the overall index. Trade-off charts and side-by-side comparison come after, to balance and inspect the shortlist.

options.why: It ranks models on this use case directly.

options.text: The leaderboard sorted by overall Quality index
options.why: It averages over many task types, so it is the wrong first filter for a math-focused app.

options.text: A trade-off chart of quality versus cost
options.why: It balances overall quality against a second metric; it does not rank models on math.
It compares two or three models you have already picked; it does not build the shortlist.

cards.question: You tick two or three models in the Microsoft Foundry model leaderboard and select **Compare**. Which **four** kinds of information does the side-by-side comparison show?
cards.answer:
- **Performance benchmarks** — quality, safety, throughput
- **Model details** — context window, training data, supported languages
- **Supported endpoints** — deployment options
- **Feature support** — function calling, structured output, vision
cards.explanation: The steps: open the Model leaderboard, check the boxes next to two or three model names, choose Compare. Unlike a trade-off chart, which plots two metrics across many models, this view goes deep on a shortlist. It shows not only how each model scores but what it brings: its context window, its endpoints, and features such as function calling.

cards.question: Name the **four** pay-per-token deployment types in Microsoft Foundry and what each one is for.
cards.answer:
- **Global Standard** — any Azure region; general workloads, highest quota; use it whenever possible
- **Data Zone Standard** — data stays in one data zone (US, EU, APAC); data zone compliance
- **Regional Standard** — a single region; regional data residency or low-volume scenarios
- **Developer** — any Azure region; fine-tuned model evaluation only
cards.explanation: Foundry's nine deployment types differ in data residency, scaling and billing. These four bill per token: you pay for what you use and reserve no capacity. The prefix sets how far data may travel, from Global (any region) through Data Zone to Regional (one region). Global Standard gives maximum capabilities, so narrow the scope only when compliance demands it. Developer is not for production at all.
cards.addition: Current docs call Regional Standard just **Standard** (SKU `Standard`), processed within an Azure geography. Developer deployments are deleted automatically after 24 hours and have no SLA or data residency guarantee.

cards.question: Name the **five** provisioned and batch deployment types in Microsoft Foundry and what each one gives you.
cards.answer:
- **Global Provisioned** — reserved **provisioned throughput units (PTUs)**, any region; predictable high throughput
- **Data Zone Provisioned** — reserved PTUs within a data zone
- **Regional Provisioned** — reserved PTUs within a single region
- **Global Batch** — any region, 50 % discount, large asynchronous jobs within 24 hours
- **Data Zone Batch** — large asynchronous batch jobs within a data zone
cards.explanation: Provisioned types reserve capacity in PTUs instead of charging per token. That reservation is what makes throughput predictable, so they suit steady, high-volume traffic. Batch types are for big asynchronous jobs where no user waits for the answer. The Global / Data Zone / Regional prefix works as for the Standard types: it only decides where data may go. Each model card lists the types that model supports.
cards.addition: Provisioned types also give lower and more consistent latency. Standard types are best effort: with high, steady volume their latency varies more.

cards.question: A Microsoft Foundry chat app must keep its data inside the **EU data zone**, may use any region within that zone, and should be billed **per token**. Which deployment type do you choose?
cards.answer: **Data Zone Standard**.
cards.explanation: Data Zone deployments keep data inside one data zone, such as the US, EU or APAC. *Standard* means pay-per-token billing. Global Standard offers the highest quota but may use any Azure region, so it breaks the compliance requirement. Regional Standard would also keep data in the EU, but ties the deployment to a single region.
cards.addition: For every deployment type, data stored at rest stays in the resource's Azure geography. The Global / Data Zone / Regional choice decides where prompts and responses are **processed** during inference.

cards.question: A Microsoft Foundry deployment must keep data inside the **EU data zone**, may use any region within that zone, and must also guarantee **predictable high throughput** for an online app. Which deployment type do you choose?
cards.answer: **Data Zone Provisioned**.
cards.explanation: Two requirements, two halves of the name: *Data Zone* keeps data in the zone (US, EU or APAC), *Provisioned* reserves PTUs for predictable throughput. Each of the other types meets only one of the two requirements.

options.why: Reserved PTUs within a data zone: residency and predictable throughput together.
Keeps data in the zone but bills per token with no reserved throughput.
Reserves PTUs but may process data in any Azure region.
Made for large asynchronous jobs, not for an online app.

cards.question: You must summarise two million archived support tickets with a Microsoft Foundry model. Results are needed within a day, data may be processed in any region, and cost must be as low as possible. Which deployment type do you choose?
cards.answer: **Global Batch**.
cards.explanation: Batch deployments run large asynchronous jobs within 24 hours at a 50 % discount. No user waits for an answer here, so giving up real-time responses costs nothing. *Global* fits because the job has no residency constraint.

options.why: Any region, 50 % discount, built for large asynchronous jobs finished within 24 hours.
Pay-per-token at full price, meant for general interactive workloads.
Reserves PTUs for steady, predictable throughput; paying for reserved capacity does not fit a one-off job.
Only for evaluating fine-tuned models.

cards.question: Put the steps of deploying a model from the **Microsoft Foundry portal** in order.
cards.answer: Model card in the **model catalog** (**Discover > Models**) → Deploy (default or custom) → **Agree and Proceed** to Marketplace terms if needed → name and type → Deploy, then the playground.
cards.explanation: The model card shows the model's specifications and the deployment types it supports. The Marketplace step appears only for models that need an Azure Marketplace subscription, common for partner and community models. Models sold directly by Azure, such as GPT-4o-mini, don't need it. When the deployment completes, the portal opens the playground, and the deployment list should show the status **Succeeded**.
items: Open the model card in the model catalog via Discover > Models
Select Deploy and choose default or custom settings
Accept the Azure Marketplace terms (Agree and Proceed) if the model requires them
Set the deployment name and deployment type
Select Deploy, then test the model in the playground

cards.question: After you select **Deploy** on a model in the Microsoft Foundry portal, which **two** ways of deploying can you choose?
cards.answer:
- **Default settings** — deploy quickly with the recommended configuration
- **Custom settings** — customize the deployment options yourself
cards.explanation: Both paths start from the Deploy button on the model card. Default settings are the fast path: the portal already preselects a fitting deployment type from the model and your environment, and the deployment name defaults to the model name. Custom settings are for when a recommendation doesn't fit, for example when compliance rules need a different deployment type than the one the portal picked, because the type decides data residency and throughput.

cards.question: Name the **two** deployment settings you configure for every model deployment in the Microsoft Foundry portal, and what each one does.
cards.answer:
- **Deployment name** — defaults to the model name; your code puts it in the `model` parameter to route requests
- **Deployment type** — preselected by the portal; decides data residency and throughput guarantees
cards.explanation: Rename a deployment when you deploy the same model more than once, for example with different settings: a meaningful name makes sure each request reaches the right one. The portal picks the deployment type from the model and your environment, and each model supports a different set of types. Managed compute deployments add two settings of their own, the VM SKU and the instance count.

explanation_images.alt: Foundry portal 'Deploy gpt-4.1' dialog with the fields Deployment name (gpt-4.1-2) and Deployment type (Global Standard)

cards.question: When you deploy a model to **managed compute** in Microsoft Foundry, which **two** extra settings do you configure?
cards.answer:
- **Virtual machine SKU** — the VM type, from the supported list; needs **Azure Machine Learning compute quota** for that SKU
- **Instance count** — how many instances run, for load distribution and redundancy
cards.explanation: Managed compute hosts the model on virtual machines you choose, so you size them yourself. Those VMs count against the subscription's Azure Machine Learning compute quota: without quota for the chosen SKU, the deployment cannot be created. Several instances share the load and keep the model reachable if one of them fails.
cards.addition: The deployment types (Global Standard, Provisioned, Batch and so on) apply only to the serverless API option. Models on managed compute don't use them.

cards.question: After a model is deployed in Microsoft Foundry, name the **three** places in the portal where you manage it, try it and get code to call it.
cards.answer:
- **Build > Models** — the deployment list; details show configuration, status, endpoint URL, keys and metrics
- **Playground** — test prompts interactively, without writing code
- **Code tab** (in the playground) — sample code in Python, C# or JavaScript to copy into your app
cards.explanation: Build > Models lists the deployments in your resource; Discover > Models is the catalog of models you could deploy. The details page also lets you change settings or delete the deployment. The playground opens by itself when a deployment completes, with the deployment preselected, and is the place for prompt engineering. The Code tab bridges those experiments to your app: its samples show authentication, endpoint configuration and request formatting.

cards.question: In the Microsoft Foundry playground, name the **message** and the **three** generation parameters you adjust to shape a deployed model's responses.
cards.answer:
- **System message** — context, tone and instructions that apply to all user inputs
- **Temperature** — creativity versus consistency
- **Max tokens** — limits the response length
- **Top-p** — nucleus sampling
cards.explanation: The system message gives the model a role for every prompt, not just one, for example "respond as a customer service representative" or "provide concise, technical explanations". The three parameters give no role; they tune how text is generated. When answers vary too much between runs, temperature is the parameter made for that trade-off between creativity and consistency; max tokens only caps the length. Trying them in the playground first shows their effect before you write code.

cards.question: Name the **three** pieces of information an application needs from the deployment details to call a model deployed in Microsoft Foundry.
cards.answer:
- **Endpoint URL** — where the application sends its requests
- **Authentication key** — secret key or token for each request; **Microsoft Entra ID** authentication is recommended for production
- **Deployment name** — goes in the `model` parameter and routes to your deployment
cards.explanation: With Entra ID, the app presents a token based on its own identity instead of a secret key. Keys work too, but Entra ID is the recommendation for production. The deployment name, not the model name, selects the deployment, which matters once one model has several. For building the requests, the portal adds SDKs, REST API documentation and code samples covering formatting, authentication and response handling.

cards.question: Name the **two** kinds of endpoint Microsoft Foundry supports for calling a deployed model, and when each one fits.
cards.answer:
- **Project endpoint** — for Foundry-specific functionality
- **OpenAI v1 endpoint** — for broad compatibility with OpenAI model APIs
cards.explanation: Choose by what the app needs. An app that uses functionality only Foundry offers calls the project endpoint. An app written against OpenAI model APIs fits the OpenAI v1 endpoint, because that endpoint exists for compatibility with those APIs. Either one is the endpoint URL from the deployment details, and in both cases the deployment name goes in the request's `model` parameter.

cards.question: Name the **four** purposes that evaluating a generative AI model serves during application development in Microsoft Foundry.
cards.answer:
- **Quality assurance** — find issues during evaluation, not in production
- **User satisfaction** — consistently helpful, appropriate responses
- **Continuous improvement** — re-evaluate as prompts, features or models change
- **Compliance and safety** — policies kept, no harmful content, privacy respected
cards.explanation: Quality assurance protects users and the organization's reputation, because problems surface before production. Evaluating for user satisfaction shows how users experience the app and where improvements make the biggest impact. Continuous improvement comes from analysing results after every prompt update, new feature or retraining. Compliance and safety also covers data protection requirements.

cards.question: How do **manual** and **automated** evaluation of a generative AI model in Microsoft Foundry differ?
cards.answer:
- **Manual evaluation** — human reviewers; time-intensive; captures subjective aspects such as user satisfaction, contextual appropriateness and brand alignment
- **Automated evaluation** — standard metrics; scales efficiently with consistent, objective measurements
cards.explanation: Neither replaces the other. Automated metrics score any number of responses the same way every time, but they can't judge whether a reply fits the brand or the situation. Human review catches exactly that, at the cost of time. Combining manual testing, automated metrics and comprehensive evaluation flows builds confidence that the model performs well and serves users safely.

cards.question: Name the **three** manual evaluation approaches, in which human reviewers assess a generative AI model's responses.
cards.answer:
- **Interactive testing** — explore the model with diverse prompts in the playground
- **Structured review** — evaluators rate responses to a set of test cases on criteria
- **User studies** — actual or representative users give feedback
cards.explanation: Interactive testing is qualitative: you note incorrect information, inappropriate tone or ignored instructions. In the Foundry playground you can test models side by side with synchronized system instructions and prompts, so differences come from the models. Structured review turns human judgement into numbers: ratings on a scale such as 1–5, aggregated across test cases. User studies reveal real-world issues controlled testing misses, such as confusing phrasing, missing context or unmet expectations.

explanation_images.alt: Foundry playground with two chat panes side by side, gpt-4.1-mini and gpt-4.1, answering the same prompt; Compare models button at the top right

cards.question: Name the **five** criteria human evaluators rate responses on in a structured review of a generative AI app.
cards.answer:
- **Relevance** — addresses the question or request
- **Informativeness** — sufficient detail and useful information
- **Engagement** — interesting and appropriately conversational
- **Accuracy** — facts and statements are correct
- **Safety** — avoids harmful, biased or inappropriate content
cards.explanation: Evaluators rate each criterion per test case, typically on a 1–5 scale; aggregated across many test cases, the ratings give a quantitative measure of overall quality. Relevance and informativeness are the easiest to mix up: one asks whether the response is on the question, the other whether it says enough to be useful. Relevance means the same as the automated metric; Safety is the human counterpart of the risk and safety metrics.

cards.question: Name the **four** generation quality metrics in Microsoft Foundry evaluation, plus the binary variant of one of them.
cards.answer:
- **Groundedness** — based on the provided context, not speculation
- **Groundedness Pro** — binary verdict: grounded or not grounded
- **Relevance** — addresses the user's question or request
- **Coherence** — flows logically with consistent ideas
- **Fluency** — linguistic correctness, natural language quality
cards.explanation: Groundedness compares the response with the context it was given, so it is the metric for apps that must not speculate. Relevance compares the response with the user's question instead. Coherence judges the logic that connects the ideas; fluency judges the language itself. Groundedness Pro's yes-or-no verdict is useful for strict factual accuracy requirements.
cards.addition: Groundedness Pro (preview) runs on the Azure AI Content Safety service and needs no judge deployment. Standard Groundedness uses your own GPT deployment as LLM judge and scores 1–5, with a default pass threshold of 3.

cards.question: Name the **six** risk and safety metrics a Microsoft Foundry evaluation uses to identify potentially harmful content.
cards.answer:
- **Self-harm content** — discussing or encouraging self-harm
- **Hateful and unfair content** — bias, discrimination, hateful statements
- **Violent content** — containing or promoting violence
- **Sexual content** — inappropriate sexual content
- **Protected material** — reproduced copyright or proprietary content
- **Indirect attack (jailbreak)** — vulnerability to manipulation attempts
cards.explanation: The first four are content harm metrics, judged by severity: their defect rate is the share of responses above a severity threshold. Protected material and indirect attack are found or not found, so their defect rate is the share of true instances. Indirect attack is the odd one out: it measures how easily the model is manipulated, not harmful content itself. Concerning results call for content filters, prompt hardening or output validation.
cards.addition: Current docs call it Indirect Attack (XPIA, cross-domain prompt injection): the jailbreak is hidden in a document or other context the model reads, not typed in by the user. It is available for model evaluation only, not for agents.

cards.question: How does a Microsoft Foundry evaluation report its results for content harm metrics such as violent or self-harm content?
cards.answer: As a **defect rate**: the percentage of responses whose severity exceeds a threshold, typically Medium.
cards.explanation: The defect rate condenses many per-response severity ratings into one number per metric. Protected material and indirect attack are calculated differently: their defect rate is simply `(true instances / total instances) × 100`, the share of responses in which the problem was found.
cards.addition: Content safety evaluators score severity 0–7: Very Low 0–1, Low 2–3, Medium 4–5, High 6–7. The default threshold is 3, so a response fails from Medium upward.

cards.question: What does a Microsoft Foundry evaluation need to calculate **AI-assisted** metrics, and what to calculate **NLP** metrics?
cards.answer:
- AI-assisted metrics — a **GPT model as evaluator** that reads and scores each response
- NLP metrics — usually **ground truth data**: expected or reference responses, no evaluator model
cards.explanation: AI-assisted metrics are not a formula: the evaluator model analyses your deployed model's responses and assigns scores against the selected criteria. NLP metrics are mathematical and compare words or word sequences with the reference. That works when a definitive correct answer exists, as in translation or classification, and is less suitable for open-ended generation where many valid responses exist.

explanation_images.alt: Foundry evaluation results table: one Fluency score per test row, marked Pass or Fail, with the evaluator's written reason next to it

cards.addition: Risk and safety evaluators are the exception: they run on Microsoft's hosted models in the Foundry Evaluation service and need no `deployment_name`. Only LLM-as-judge quality evaluators such as coherence and fluency use your own deployment.

cards.question: Name the **five** NLP metrics that Microsoft Foundry evaluation calculates mathematically against ground truth data.
cards.answer:
- **F1-score** — ratio of shared words, balancing **precision** (no incorrect words) and **recall** (important words included)
- **BLEU** — compares **n-grams** (word sequences) with a reference; machine translation
- **METEOR** — extends BLEU with synonyms, stemming, paraphrasing
- **ROUGE** — favours recall over precision; summarization
- **GLEU** — Google-BLEU, sentence-level variant
cards.explanation: Choose by task. ROUGE suits summarization, where covering the key points matters more than avoiding extra words. BLEU is the common metric for machine translation; METEOR makes that comparison more flexible, so synonyms and paraphrases still count. F1-score fits text classification and information retrieval. BLEU stands for Bilingual Evaluation Understudy, ROUGE for Recall-Oriented Understudy for Gisting Evaluation.

cards.question: Which Microsoft Foundry portal feature runs systematic evaluations with test datasets and several metrics at once, and which **three** bases can such an evaluation have?
cards.answer:
**Evaluation**:
- **Model** — a deployed model answers your prompts; outputs are generated during the evaluation
- **Agent** — an agent's responses to user-defined prompts
- **Dataset** — pre-generated outputs already in the test dataset
cards.explanation: Model and Agent need a dataset that supplies the inputs, and you configure the metrics, the field mappings for the data and, for a model, its system prompt. Dataset is the case where your file already holds prompts and the responses your app generated: nothing is generated, only the scoring runs. The job runs asynchronously, processing each row against the selected metrics, and the results show aggregate scores plus the details of each test prompt.

cards.question: Name the **three** options for supplying test data when you evaluate a model or agent in the Microsoft Foundry **Evaluation** feature.
cards.answer:
- **Upload new dataset** — a **CSV or JSONL** file from local storage
- **Use existing dataset** — one previously uploaded to the project
- **Generate synthetic dataset** — sample data created from a topic description
cards.explanation: Use existing dataset reuses data already uploaded to the project, so a second model can be scored on the same test cases.
