The Foundry playground tests only the agent itself and does not simulate the published experience. Only after these local tests pass do you provision Azure resources, deploy the proxy and register it in Teams.

options.why: It is the Agents Toolkit's local testing environment that simulates Teams; debug mode opens it in the browser.

options.text: The agent playground in the Foundry portal
options.why: It tests the Foundry agent directly and does not simulate the published Teams experience or run your proxy's middleware.

options.text: Teams **Apps > Manage your apps > Upload a custom app**
options.why: That installs a finished publishing package in a real Teams client; it is how you test the package from direct Foundry publishing.
It is a Foundry publishing channel, a browser interface for demos of a published agent, not a local Teams simulation.

cards.addition: Agents Playground needs no Microsoft 365 developer tenant, no tunneling service such as Ngrok and no app or bot registration. It can also simulate scenarios with mock data and custom activity triggers.

cards.question: Compare **direct publishing from the Microsoft Foundry portal** with a **Microsoft 365 Agents Toolkit proxy** for bringing an agent into Teams: how do they differ on the **five** compared aspects?
cards.answer:
- **Setup time** — minutes vs. hours to days
- **Code required** — none vs. a proxy application
- **Customization** — limited vs. extensive
- **Debugging** — Foundry portal vs. full IDE debugging
- **Best for** — standard deployments vs. complex enterprise needs
cards.explanation: Direct publishing handles the majority of integration scenarios, so it is the default. Production alone is no reason for the toolkit: direct publishing with organization scope is the course's path for production deployments. Switch to the proxy only when a specific requirement, such as custom SSO or middleware, justifies hours of setup and a proxy application in your deployment.

cards.question: What is **Microsoft Work IQ**, and which protocol is it built on?
cards.answer: A **CLI and server** that connects AI agents and assistants to your **Microsoft 365 Copilot data**, so they can query workplace information in natural language. It is built on the **Model Context Protocol (MCP)** and acts as an MCP server for Microsoft 365 data.
cards.explanation: The point is context: an agent that knows what your manager said about a deadline, which documents cover Q4 planning or who works on Project Alpha gives more relevant and accurate answers. Because Work IQ speaks MCP, any MCP-capable assistant can discover its tools and call them. Work IQ APIs reached general availability in June 2026, and Work IQ also supports remote MCP server connections to external MCP-compatible endpoints.

cards.question: Name the **five** kinds of Microsoft 365 data that **Microsoft Work IQ** gives AI agents access to.
cards.answer:
- **Emails** — search messages, find communications from specific people
- **Meetings** — check the calendar, retrieve meeting notes and decisions
- **Documents** — find and search files in SharePoint and OneDrive
- **Teams messages** — summarize channel discussions, find conversations
- **People** — identify team members and collaborators on projects
cards.explanation: Together these cover the questions a workplace agent typically gets: "Summarize today's messages in the Engineering channel" draws on Teams messages, "Who is working on Project Alpha?" on People, "What did my manager say about the project deadline?" on Emails or Meetings. Documents is the only type that names where it lives: SharePoint and OneDrive. All five come from the user's Microsoft 365 Copilot data, so the agent answers from the organization's real context.

cards.question: Name the **three** kinds of capabilities a **Model Context Protocol (MCP) server** can expose to an AI agent.
cards.answer:
- **Tools** — actions the agent can take, such as searching documents or sending messages
- **Resources** — data sources the agent can query
- **Prompts** — predefined templates for common queries
cards.explanation: MCP is an open protocol that connects AI assistants to external data sources and tools. When you configure an MCP server for an agent, the agent discovers which tools and resources the server offers and uses them to fulfill user requests. The line between the first two is action versus data: a Tool does something, a Resource is something to read. Work IQ is one such MCP server, designed specifically for Microsoft 365 data.

cards.question: Name the **two** modes **Microsoft Work IQ** runs in, and when you would use each.
cards.answer:
- **CLI mode** — you run queries yourself in the terminal (`workiq ask -q "…"`); for quick ad-hoc queries and scripts
- **MCP server mode** — an AI assistant such as GitHub Copilot in VS Code calls Work IQ's tools automatically when relevant
cards.explanation: Both modes read the same Microsoft 365 data with the same permissions; only who triggers the query differs. In CLI mode you ask explicitly, which suits one-off questions or scripts without opening an IDE. In MCP server mode you just ask your assistant, for example "What requirements did Sarah share about the authentication feature?", and the assistant decides on its own when to query Work IQ. Meeting context then flows into its suggestions without any commands.

cards.question: Name the **three** ways to install or configure **Microsoft Work IQ**, and the command you must run before its first use.
cards.answer:
- **npm** — `npm install -g @microsoft/workiq`, or run without installing via `npx -y @microsoft/workiq mcp`
- **GitHub Copilot CLI plugin** — `/plugin install workiq@copilot-plugins`
- **VS Code MCP configuration** — a `workiq` server entry: command `npx`, args `-y @microsoft/workiq mcp`
- **Before first use** — `workiq accept-eula` accepts the End User License Agreement
cards.explanation: Both the npx command and the VS Code entry end with `mcp`, the argument that runs Work IQ as an MCP server. In GitHub Copilot CLI you add the plugins marketplace once (`/plugin marketplace add github/copilot-plugins`), install the plugin and restart the CLI. The VS Code entry's `"tools": ["*"]` makes every Work IQ tool available to the assistant. Whichever route you take, the EULA must be accepted before Work IQ answers its first query.

cards.question: Name the **three** prerequisites for using **Microsoft Work IQ**.
cards.answer:
- **Node.js** — when you run the CLI locally
- **Microsoft 365 Copilot license** — on a Microsoft 365 subscription
- **Administrative consent** — for the Work IQ application in your Microsoft Entra tenant
cards.explanation: Admin consent is the one a developer usually cannot grant alone. Work IQ accesses organization-wide Microsoft 365 data, so a tenant administrator must approve the application; if you are not one, request access from your IT department. The Copilot license is just as hard a requirement: standard Microsoft 365 accounts without Copilot do not work with Work IQ.

cards.question: **Microsoft Work IQ** inherits the security model of Microsoft 365 Copilot. Name its **four** security properties.
cards.answer:
- **Permission-based access** — only data the user may already view
- **No data storage** — retrieves on demand, keeps no Microsoft 365 data
- **Enterprise security** — all access follows the organization's security policies
- **Admin visibility** — administrators can monitor and control usage
cards.explanation: Work IQ brings no security model of its own; it inherits Microsoft 365 Copilot's. So an agent that uses Work IQ never sees more than the person asking it, and no copy of Microsoft 365 data builds up that would need separate protection. Every access stays inside the organization's existing security policies, and administrators can monitor and control how Work IQ is used.

cards.question: A developer asks an assistant connected to **Microsoft Work IQ** to summarize an HR document they have no permission to open. Admin consent for Work IQ was granted for the tenant. What happens?
cards.answer: Work IQ **cannot access the document**: it queries Microsoft Graph with the developer's own authenticated identity.
cards.explanation: Work IQ has no access path of its own. Every query runs through Microsoft Graph as the signed-in user, so documents that user cannot view stay out of reach, each query is auditable by the organization, and data protection policies apply. Admin consent is required because Work IQ touches organization-wide data, but it approves the application; it does not widen what any single user can see.

options.text: Work IQ cannot access the document, because it queries Microsoft Graph with the developer's identity
options.why: Permission-based access: Work IQ only reaches data the signed-in user already has permission to view.

options.text: Work IQ returns the document, because the tenant-wide admin consent grants it organization-wide access
options.why: Admin consent lets the Work IQ application run in the tenant; it does not add permissions to any user.

options.text: Work IQ answers from its stored copy of the tenant's Microsoft 365 data
options.why: Work IQ stores no Microsoft 365 data; it retrieves information on demand under the user's permissions.

options.text: Work IQ returns the document but logs the query for administrators to review
options.why: Queries are auditable, but auditing never grants access to data the user cannot view.

cards.question: A developer wants **GitHub Copilot in Visual Studio Code** to pull requirements from recent Microsoft 365 meetings and emails into its answers automatically, without running any commands. How should **Microsoft Work IQ** be used?
cards.answer: Run Work IQ in **MCP server mode** by adding it to the VS Code MCP configuration; Copilot then calls its tools when relevant.
cards.explanation: The difference between the two modes is who triggers the query. In CLI mode the developer runs `workiq ask` in the terminal, which suits scripts and quick one-off questions. In MCP server mode the assistant discovers Work IQ's tools and decides itself when to call them, so the developer just asks Copilot and the meeting context arrives in the chat. Both modes read the same data with the same permissions.

options.text: Add Work IQ as an MCP server in the VS Code MCP configuration
options.why: In MCP server mode the AI assistant calls Work IQ's tools automatically when a question needs workplace context.

options.text: Run `workiq ask -q "…"` in the terminal for each question
options.why: That is CLI mode: it works, but the developer has to run every query explicitly.

options.text: Publish a Foundry agent to Microsoft Teams with organization scope
options.why: Publishing makes an agent available to Teams users; it does not give GitHub Copilot in VS Code access to Microsoft 365 data.

options.text: Scaffold a project with the Microsoft 365 Agents Toolkit
options.why: The Agents Toolkit is for custom SSO, middleware and multi-environment deployment of an agent, not for feeding Microsoft 365 data to Copilot in VS Code.

cards.question: The Microsoft Foundry playground does not simulate the published experience. Name the **four** things you verify by testing a published Foundry agent in Microsoft Teams.
cards.answer:
- **Rendering** — the Teams UI renders responses correctly
- **Authentication** — auth flows work as expected
- **Response times** — acceptable in production
- **Agent identity permissions** — the published identity has what it needs
cards.explanation: The playground tests the agent itself, but not the published path. After publishing, the agent runs under its own Microsoft Entra identity, separate from your development project, and Azure Bot Service carries the messages between Teams and the agent. Problems in that path only show up in Teams. Do not test alone: colleagues phrase questions differently and spot confusing responses you would miss. Also try the Teams desktop, web and mobile clients, because some issues are platform-specific.

cards.question: You published a Microsoft Foundry agent to Teams, but it **does not respond at all** to messages there. What do you check first?
cards.answer:
Check the **Azure Bot Service**: verify the resource exists in the Azure portal and read its logs, then confirm the agent is published and the package was uploaded.

Causes: Bot Service **not running**, **misconfigured**, or **network issues** between Teams and the agent.
cards.explanation: Azure Bot Service is created when you publish from the Foundry portal and routes every message between Microsoft 365 and the agent. If it is missing, stopped or wrongly configured, or the network between Teams and the agent fails, no message reaches the agent and nothing comes back. The other symptoms have their own fixes: failing tools need RBAC roles on the published identity, an agent users cannot find needs the right scope or approval, slow answers need simpler instructions or tools.

options.text: Verify the Azure Bot Service resource exists and check its logs for errors
options.why: Bot Service carries every message between Teams and the agent; if it is missing, stopped or misconfigured, nothing comes back.

options.text: Assign RBAC roles to the published agent identity on the resources its tools use
options.why: That fixes tools that work in Foundry but fail in Teams; the agent still answers in that case.

options.text: Verify admin approval in the Microsoft 365 admin center
options.why: Pending approval stops users from finding an organization-scope agent; it does not make a reachable agent silent.
That addresses slow responses, not missing ones.

cards.question: Users **cannot find** your published Microsoft Foundry agent in Teams. Name the **three** possible causes and the fix for each.
cards.answer:
- **Wrong publish scope** — for shared scope, share the direct link with users
- **Admin approval pending** (organization scope) — verify approval in the Microsoft 365 admin center
- **Tenant policies block custom apps** — check the tenant settings for custom app permissions
cards.explanation: All three are about distribution, not about the agent itself — it may work perfectly for you. A shared-scope agent is not listed for the whole organization, so others need the link. An organization-scope agent only appears for everyone after an administrator approves it. And even then, a tenant that does not allow custom apps keeps it hidden.

cards.question: Your Microsoft Foundry agent published to Teams **answers slowly**. Name the **three** possible causes and the fix for each.
cards.answer:
- **Complex agent instructions** — simplify them where possible
- **Tools that query large data sets** — optimize the tool configurations
- **Network latency** — test from different network locations to isolate it
cards.explanation: Each cause sits in a different place: the instructions make the model process longer, the tools spend time fetching data, the network adds time on the way. Testing from several locations tells you whether the delay follows the network or the agent. Acceptable response time is one of the things you check in Teams after publishing, because the playground cannot show production latency.

cards.question: You monitor a Microsoft Foundry agent published to Teams. Name the **four** metrics the Foundry portal shows and the **four** things Application Insights integration adds.
cards.answer:
Foundry portal metrics:
- **Request volume** and patterns
- **Response times**
- **Error rates**
- **Tool invocation statistics**

Application Insights:
- **Trace** individual conversations
- **Analyze error patterns**
- **Measure end-to-end latency**
- **Set up alerts** for anomalies
cards.explanation: Monitoring should catch issues before users report them. The Foundry metrics show trends, so review them regularly. Application Insights goes down to single conversations, but only if you configured the integration. The third source is users: set up a Teams channel or email address for feedback and review it periodically. When you fix something, update the agent in the Foundry portal and republish; for organization scope, tenant policies decide whether the update needs re-approval.

cards.question: Put the steps in order to take a document-grounded agent from the Microsoft Foundry portal into Microsoft Teams.
cards.answer: Create agent → instructions → **Upload files** under Tools → test in playground → **Publish to Teams and Microsoft 365 Copilot** → scope and Submit.
cards.explanation: Uploading files in the **Tools** section gives the agent file search over the documents. Testing in the playground comes before publishing: if Teams answers turn generic later, the checks are whether file search is enabled, the documents were uploaded and indexed, and the playground answers correctly. After **Submit**, the agent appears in Teams under **Apps** → **Your agents**, sometimes only after 1–2 minutes.
items: Create a project and an agent in the new Foundry portal (**Start building** → **Create agent**)
Set the agent's **Instructions** and select **Save**
In the **Tools** section, select **Upload files**, attach the documents and select **Attach**
Ask knowledge questions in the playground to check the answers come from the documents
Select **Publish** → **Publish to Teams and Microsoft 365 Copilot**, fill in the app details and icons, then **Prepare Agent**
Select **Continue the in-product publishing flow**, choose the publish scope and select **Submit**

cards.question: When you publish a Microsoft Foundry agent to Teams, what does the portal create for you automatically, and which **two icons** and which **app scope** do you set in the Teams app form?
cards.answer:
- Generated: an **Azure Bot Service**, a **Teams app manifest** and a downloadable **app package** with icons and configuration
- **Color icon** — 192×192 PNG, full color
- **Outline icon** — 32×32 PNG, white outline on transparent background, shown in the Teams sidebar
- App scope: **Personal** for one-to-one chat, optionally **Team** for channels
cards.explanation: You never build the bot or the manifest yourself; the publishing flow does it. If direct publishing returns a **400** error and your Microsoft 365 account may publish custom apps, the **Download & customize** tab is the fallback. A manual upload fails if the icons have the wrong sizes, the `manifest.zip` is corrupted or the Teams admin has disabled custom app uploads. An agent that installs but does not answer: wait about 30 seconds and check that the Azure Bot Service was created.

cards.question: Your Microsoft Foundry agent is already published to Teams. How do you make it available in **Microsoft 365 Copilot**, and how do users reach it there?
cards.answer:
- The **same publishing flow** (**Publish to Teams and Microsoft 365 Copilot**) serves both
- The agent becomes a **Copilot extension** (declarative agent)
- Users **@mention** it in Copilot or pick it under **Your agents** in the agent store
- Needs a **Microsoft 365 Copilot license**
cards.explanation: One publish puts the agent in Teams and Copilot, and Copilot routes the user's query to it. Users get the agent's knowledge alongside Copilot's own capabilities and switch between the two seamlessly; Teams alone works with a standard Microsoft 365 account. With **shared** scope (the lab's Teams section calls it **Individual scope**) the agent is available at once; with **organization** scope an admin first approves it in the Microsoft 365 admin center under **Requests**, then it appears under **Built by your org**. Deleting the agent in Foundry also removes its Azure Bot Service and published deployments, and the Copilot extension becomes inactive.

cards.question: Put the steps in order to set up **Work IQ** and run a Python Microsoft Foundry agent app that uses it.
cards.answer: `npm install -g @microsoft/workiq` → `workiq accept-eula` → test with `workiq ask` → venv + `pip install` → set `.env` → `python workiq_lab.py`.
cards.explanation: Work IQ **only works** with Microsoft 365 Copilot-licensed accounts, and organizational accounts also need **admin consent**. The test query proves both before you write code: on *Admin consent required* it shows a consent URL to send to your IT admin; on *No M365 Copilot license* you cannot continue. You copy the project endpoint in VS Code via the **Foundry Toolkit**: right-click the project → **Copy Endpoint**. The lab creates no Azure resources, because Work IQ runs on your Microsoft 365 license.
items: Install the Work IQ CLI globally: npm install -g @microsoft/workiq
Accept the End User License Agreement: workiq accept-eula
Test it: workiq ask -q "What meetings do I have today?"
Create and activate a Python virtual environment, then pip install -r requirements.txt
Set PROJECT_ENDPOINT and MODEL_DEPLOYMENT_NAME in the .env file
Run the app: python workiq_lab.py

cards.question: A Python app gives a Microsoft Foundry prompt agent the tools of the local **Work IQ MCP server** and answers a query with the Responses API. Put the steps in order.
cards.answer: List the MCP tools → wrap them as **`FunctionTool`** and create the agent version → send the query with `agent_reference` → run each `function_call` over MCP → return **`FunctionCallOutput`** until no calls remain → delete the agent version.
cards.explanation: The agent never calls Work IQ itself. It only **requests** a function call, and the app bridges it: it runs the tool over MCP and feeds the result back with the matching `call_id` and `previous_response_id`. The loop ends when a response has no pending function calls; `response.output_text` then holds the answer. The app opens a **new MCP session per operation** instead of keeping a persistent connection. This Responses API pattern replaces the old Runs/Threads pattern.
items: Launch the server with StdioServerParameters (npx -y @microsoft/workiq mcp) and call session.list_tools()
Wrap each MCP tool in a FunctionTool and create the agent with agents.create_version and a PromptAgentDefinition
Create a conversation with the user's query and call responses.create with the agent_reference
For each function_call output item, run session.call_tool(item.name, kwargs) in a new MCP session
Send the results as FunctionCallOutput items with previous_response_id, repeating until no function calls remain
On exit, remove the agent with agents.delete_version

cards.question: A Microsoft Foundry agent must compare what employees **discuss** about the expense policy in emails, meetings and Teams with what the **official policy documents** say. Which **two** IQ sources does it combine, which side does each provide, and what must the Foundry project have for the documents?
cards.answer:
- **Work IQ** — workplace data: emails, meetings, Teams discussions (what people actually do and say)
- **Foundry IQ** — the knowledge base: official docs, policies, procedures
- Foundry IQ needs **Azure AI Search** with an indexed knowledge base in the project
cards.explanation: In the lab's *Combined Intelligence* scenario one agent searches both sources. It compares informal discussion with official documentation, finds gaps or contradictions, and labels each source in its summary. Neither source alone is enough: Work IQ shows current practice, Foundry IQ shows the documented rule. Together they give complete context for a decision. Beyond the Foundry project itself, only the Foundry IQ side needs an extra Azure resource; Work IQ runs on the user's Microsoft 365 Copilot license.

cards.question: What Azure resource does the Foundry portal automatically create when you publish an agent to Microsoft Teams?
cards.answer: An **Azure Bot Service** resource.
cards.explanation: The Bot Service routes messages between Microsoft 365 and the Foundry agent. The publishing wizard creates it in your subscription, registers a Microsoft Entra ID application and generates the Microsoft 365 publishing package. That is why the **Microsoft.BotService** resource provider must be registered in the subscription before you publish.

options.why: Units 2.5.2 and 2.5.3 list no Functions app among the resources the publishing wizard creates.
Unit 2.5.2: publishing to Microsoft 365 creates an Azure Bot Service resource that routes messages between Microsoft 365 and your agent; unit 2.5.3 shows the Create an Azure Bot Service step.
Unit 2.5.3 names Cosmos DB only as a resource a tool might access, which then needs RBAC roles for the agent identity.
Units 2.5.2 and 2.5.3 never mention Logic Apps; message routing is the Bot Service's job.

cards.question: What is the main difference between shared scope and organization scope when publishing an agent?
cards.answer: **Organization scope requires admin approval** before the agent is available to all users.
cards.explanation: Shared scope is available immediately without approval and appears under **Your agents** in Teams; it suits personal testing and small pilots. Organization scope makes the agent available to the whole tenant under **Built by your org**, but only after an admin selects **Approve request and activate** in the Microsoft 365 admin center (Agents > All > Requested). It suits production.

options.text: Shared scope requires more Azure resources
options.why: Unit 2.5.3: the wizard creates the Bot Service, Entra app and package before you pick the scope in step 5; the scopes differ only in distribution and approval.

options.text: Organization scope requires admin approval before the agent is available to all users
options.why: Unit 2.5.2's scope table: shared is available immediately without admin approval, organization is available to everyone in the tenant and requires admin approval.

options.text: Shared scope only works in the Foundry playground
options.why: Unit 2.5.2: a shared-scope agent appears under Your agents in Teams, not in the playground.

options.text: Organization scope provides better agent performance
options.why: Unit 2.5.6 traces slow responses to complex instructions, tools that query large data sets and network latency, never to the publish scope.

cards.question: What happens to tool permissions when you publish an agent from Foundry to Teams?
cards.answer: The published agent gets a **new identity** and needs its **permissions reassigned**.
cards.explanation: Publishing creates a distinct Microsoft Entra agent identity, separate from the development project. Permissions granted to the project identity don't transfer. Tools that worked in the playground then fail in Teams until you assign RBAC roles to the published agent identity on each resource it uses, such as Azure AI Search or a storage account.

options.text: Permissions are automatically transferred to the published agent
options.why: Unit 2.5.2: development-time permissions on your project identity don't transfer automatically.
Unit 2.5.3: tools keep working once the new identity has the right RBAC roles; you test them in Teams after publishing.

options.text: The published agent gets a new identity and needs permissions reassigned
options.why: Units 2.5.2 and 2.5.3: publishing creates a distinct agent identity, and you assign RBAC roles to it on the resources its tools access.

options.text: Permissions only work in organization scope
options.why: Unit 2.5.3: you reassign RBAC roles to the new identity the same way for either scope; scope only controls who finds the agent and whether an admin must approve it.

cards.question: What is Microsoft Work IQ?
cards.answer: A **CLI and MCP server** that connects AI agents to Microsoft 365 data.
cards.explanation: Work IQ lets agents query emails, meetings, documents, Teams messages and people in natural language. It runs in CLI mode (`workiq ask -q "…"`) for scripts and quick queries, or in MCP server mode so an assistant such as GitHub Copilot calls its tools itself. It reads data through Microsoft Graph with the user's own identity, so it sees only what the user may see.

options.text: A machine learning model for workplace analytics
options.why: Unit 2.5.5: Work IQ retrieves Microsoft 365 data on demand; it is a connector, not a model.

options.text: A CLI and MCP server that connects AI agents to Microsoft 365 data
options.why: Unit 2.5.5: Work IQ is a command-line interface and server built on the Model Context Protocol that connects AI assistants to Microsoft 365 Copilot data.
Unit 2.5.5: Teams messages are one of the data sources Work IQ reads, so it complements Teams.

options.text: A Visual Studio Code extension for building agents
options.why: Unit 2.5.4: that describes the Microsoft 365 Agents Toolkit; unit 2.5.5 adds Work IQ to VS Code only as an MCP server entry.

cards.question: When should you consider using the Microsoft 365 Agents Toolkit instead of direct publishing from Foundry?
cards.answer: When you need **custom SSO**, **middleware logic**, or **multi-environment deployment**.
cards.explanation: The toolkit builds a proxy app between Teams or Copilot and the Foundry agent: Teams/Copilot → proxy app → Foundry agent. The proxy controls every step of the message flow and adds IDE debugging and CI/CD pipelines. The price is code and hours to days of setup, against minutes for direct publishing. Direct publishing still handles most scenarios.

options.why: Unit 2.5.4: direct publishing handles the majority of scenarios; organization scope in 2.5.2 is the production path without the toolkit.

options.text: When you need custom SSO, middleware logic, or multi-environment deployment
options.why: Units 2.5.2 and 2.5.4: consider the Agents Toolkit for custom single sign-on, advanced middleware logic or multi-environment deployment pipelines.
Unit 2.5.3: shared scope is an option of the direct Foundry publishing wizard itself.

options.text: When your agent doesn't use any tools
options.why: Unit 2.5.4 ties the choice to SSO, middleware and deployment needs, not to whether the agent uses tools.

cards.question: What is a **workflow** in Microsoft Foundry, and what is it built from?
cards.answer:
- A **visual, declarative** way to orchestrate AI-driven actions without writing code
- Built from **connected nodes**, each with one function: invoke an agent, evaluate a condition, manage data or talk to the user
- The platform manages **execution and state**
cards.explanation: You describe what should happen and when; Foundry runs the steps and keeps track of state. The arranged nodes form the execution path, so they decide how a request moves through the system and where decisions are made. That fits business processes that mix AI reasoning, logic and user interaction. The screenshot shows a group chat workflow: two agents, Set variable nodes, and an If/Else that ends the run, sends a message or loops back with Go to.

explanation_images.alt: Group chat workflow in the Foundry designer: Start, Set variable, student-agent, teacher-agent, Set variable, If/Else condition branching to End, Send message, or Go to back to the student agent

cards.question: A single support agent in Microsoft Foundry handles complex, ambiguous tickets poorly. You want separate agents for classification, decision-making and resolution, and a person must be asked when the agents' confidence is low. What do you build?
cards.answer: A **workflow** that orchestrates the specialized agents and can pause for human input or escalate.
cards.explanation: Single-agent solutions often struggle with complex or ambiguous tasks. A workflow combines agents with different responsibilities into one process, which makes the automation more robust and scalable. Workflows also balance automation with oversight: when confidence is low or context is missing, they pause, request human input or escalate the decision. Real systems need reliability and control as much as efficiency.

options.text: A workflow that chains the specialized agents and pauses for human input or escalation
options.why: Workflows coordinate multiple agents and support pausing, human input and escalation when confidence is low.

options.text: One agent with longer instructions and more tools
options.why: It stays a single agent, the setup that struggles with complex, ambiguous tasks, and it adds no step that pauses the process for a person.

options.text: A guardrail configured on the existing agent
options.why: Guardrails restrict what one agent may say or do; they do not split work across agents or route a case to a human.

options.text: A knowledge base attached to the existing agent
options.why: A knowledge base gives the agent more grounding data; it does not coordinate several agents or escalate low-confidence cases.

cards.question: Name the **three** predefined workflow patterns Microsoft Foundry offers for orchestrating agents.
cards.answer:
- **Sequential** — fixed step-by-step path; each node passes its output to the next
- **Human-in-the-loop** — pauses for user input or approval, then resumes
- **Group chat** — control shifts dynamically between multiple agents
cards.explanation: The patterns differ in how decisions are made, how data flows and whether a person takes part. Sequential suits pipelines such as validate input → enrich data → generate a response; it is predictable and the easiest place to start. Human-in-the-loop balances automation with oversight. Group chat drops the fixed path: agents build on each other's outputs and adapt to changing inputs. Recognise the scenario's pattern before you start designing the workflow.

cards.question: In Microsoft Foundry, you build a customer support workflow in which several specialized agents (billing, technical, account) collaborate. Which agent handles the request next should depend on context and intermediate results, not on a fixed order. Which workflow pattern fits?
cards.answer: A **group chat** workflow.
cards.explanation: Group chat is the pattern for dynamic orchestration across multiple agents: control moves between them based on context, rules or intermediate results, and each agent can build on the others' outputs. That is what complex, multi-domain requests such as customer support or multi-domain question answering need. A sequential workflow would force every request through the same fixed chain of steps.

options.why: Control shifts between specialized agents based on context, rules or intermediate results.
Every node runs in a fixed order; it cannot hand control to whichever agent fits the request.
It adds pauses for a person's input or approval; it does not route work between agents.

options.text: A single agent with one combined set of instructions
options.why: Single-agent solutions often struggle with complex or ambiguous tasks; combining specialized agents is what workflows are for.

cards.question: A Microsoft Foundry workflow must not issue a refund until a person has confirmed it. Which workflow pattern do you use, and how does it behave at that point?
cards.answer: **Human-in-the-loop**: the workflow explicitly **asks a question**, **waits** for the response, then **resumes** based on that input.
cards.explanation: This pattern balances automation with oversight. Typical uses are approvals, confirmations, and situations where a person must supply missing context. The other two patterns never stop for a person: a sequential workflow runs its nodes in a fixed order, and a group chat passes control between agents based on context, rules or intermediate results.

cards.question: Name the **five** main node types of the Microsoft Foundry workflow builder.
cards.answer:
- **Invoke** — calls an existing or new AI agent
- **Flow** — controls the execution path (branch, jump, loop)
- **Data transformation** — manipulates data and manages variables
- **Basic chat** — sends messages to the user or asks for input
- **End** — concludes the workflow, optionally returning a result or status
cards.explanation: Invoke nodes do the AI work: classification, reasoning, recommendations, returning free text or structured output such as JSON. The other four carry the orchestration. Flow nodes let the workflow adapt to different inputs, Data transformation nodes make sure information reaches later steps correctly, and Basic chat nodes are usually paired with variables that capture the user's reply. Variables give all nodes shared state, so effective automation needs every node type, not just agents.
cards.addition: The Foundry docs group the same nodes slightly differently: **Agent** (invoke an agent), **Logic** (if/else, go to, for each), **Data transformation**, and **Basic chat** with its two actions **Send message** and **Ask a question**.

cards.question: Name the **three** Flow nodes that control the execution path of a Microsoft Foundry workflow.
cards.answer:
- **If/Else** — branches execution based on conditions
- **Go To** — jumps to another node in the workflow
- **For Each** — loops over a list, running the same actions for each item
cards.explanation: Flow nodes make a workflow react to different inputs instead of always running the same straight line. If/Else picks one of several paths, for example by checking an agent's structured output or confidence score. Go To moves execution to another node instead of the next one in line. For Each repeats the same steps per item, so a list of support tickets needs no duplicated nodes.

cards.question: Name the **three** Data transformation nodes of a Microsoft Foundry workflow.
cards.answer:
- **Set Variable** — assigns a value to a variable for later use
- **Reset Variable** — clears or reinitializes a variable
- **Parse value** — extracts data from structured outputs or converts values to another format
cards.explanation: Data transformation nodes manipulate data and manage variables so that information reaches the following steps in the right shape. Variables are the workflow's shared state: an agent's result or a user's reply stored in one step can drive a decision or trigger an action later. Parse value is the one to reach for when an agent returns structured output, such as JSON, and a later node needs only one field of it.

explanation_images.alt: Foundry workflow designer: the plus icon below Start opens 'Add a workflow action', listing Invoke agent under Invoke, and Set variable, Reset variable and Parse value under Data transformation; Visualizer, YAML and Code tabs at the top

cards.question: Partway through a Microsoft Foundry workflow, the customer must be asked for their order number, and the reply must be kept for a later agent step. Which node type asks the question?
cards.answer: A **Basic chat** node, paired with a variable that captures the reply.
cards.explanation: Basic chat nodes are the workflow's direct line to the user: they send messages or ask questions to collect input. The answer lands in a variable, and from there it can steer an If/Else branch or be passed to an agent later in the workflow. Agents reason over input, but asking the user and waiting for the reply is a chat node's job.

options.why: Basic chat nodes send messages to the user or ask questions to collect input, usually saving the reply in a variable.
Invoke calls an AI agent for reasoning or classification; it does not pause to collect input from the user.
Set Variable assigns a value the workflow already has; it cannot ask the user for one.
If/Else branches on a condition over existing data; it does not collect new input.
End concludes the workflow and can return a final result; it does not ask anything.

cards.question: You build a workflow in the Microsoft Foundry visual designer. How do you start it, keep your changes, and test it?
cards.answer:
- **Start** from a blank canvas or a **predefined pattern**, such as sequential
- **Save manually** and often — workflows are **not saved automatically**
- **Test** in the **chat window**, because workflows run in a conversational context
cards.explanation: The designer lays nodes out in execution order; you move nodes, insert steps and inspect their settings directly on the canvas. Unsaved edits are lost, so saving regularly is what preserves each version of the design. Running the workflow in the chat window shows how inputs move through the nodes, so you can check each step before adding complexity. In larger workflows the canvas makes branches and decision points easy to trace.
cards.addition: Microsoft Foundry retires workflows on **December 1, 2026**. New workflows should use **Microsoft Agent Framework**; existing ones migrate by exporting their YAML definition. Azure Logic Apps is the alternative for a visual low-code designer.

cards.question: You want an AI agent to classify incoming requests as one step of a Microsoft Foundry workflow. How do you add it, what can you configure for it, and what does it exchange with the workflow?
cards.answer:
- Insert an **Invoke agent** node
- It references an **existing agent** from the project or **creates a new one** in the designer
- Its editor configures **tools, knowledge bases, memory and guardrails**
- The workflow passes it **context** (user input, earlier variables) and uses its **response** in later steps
cards.explanation: Agents are the reasoning components of a workflow: they bring AI-driven decisions, classification and response generation into a larger orchestration. Each agent gets its own purpose, model, prompt and tools, so one workflow can combine several specialized capabilities. The editor settings tailor that agent's behavior to what this workflow needs, and the context it receives is what lets it react to the user and to earlier steps.

cards.question: In a Microsoft Foundry workflow, an agent's reply decides which branch an If/Else node takes. How do you make that reply predictable, and where do you set it up?
cards.answer: Configure **structured output**: define a response format such as a **JSON schema** in the parameters of the **Details** tab of the **Invoke agent** editor.
cards.explanation: Besides natural language responses, an agent can return structured output. A response format such as a JSON schema ensures the output always follows a predictable shape. That matters most when the agent's response drives control flow — routing logic, or assigning values to variables in later nodes. The screenshot shows the choice in the Text format list: Text, JSON Object or JSON Schema.

explanation_images.alt: Details tab of the Invoke agent editor: the Parameters panel next to the model shows Temperature, Top P and a Text format list with Text, JSON Object and JSON Schema.

cards.question: In a Microsoft Foundry workflow, a later If/Else node and a second agent both need the output of an **Invoke agent** node. Where do you configure that this output is saved so they can use it?
cards.answer: In the **Action settings** of the Invoke agent node, by storing the output in a **variable**.
cards.explanation: Once the output sits in a variable, it can be referenced anywhere later in the workflow. That is how an agent influences decisions, triggers conditional branches or feeds input to another agent. The Details tab of the same editor defines what shape the output has; Action settings defines where it is saved.

explanation_images.alt: Action settings tab of the Invoke agent node: Input message System.LastMessage, the agent output message saved as Local.TextOutput and the JSON output saved as Local.JsonOutput.

options.text: The Action settings of the Invoke agent node
options.why: This is where the agent's output is stored in a variable for later nodes.

options.text: The parameters on the Details tab of the Invoke agent editor
options.why: They define the response format, such as a JSON schema, not where the output is stored.

options.text: A Reset Variable node placed after the agent
options.why: Reset Variable clears or reinitializes a variable; it does not capture the agent's output.

options.text: The End node of the workflow
options.why: The End node only marks the conclusion and can return a final result; nothing after it can use the value.

cards.question: Several Microsoft Foundry workflows must all classify incoming requests the same way, then resolve them differently. How do you design the agents?
cards.answer: **Reuse** one **categorization agent** in every workflow, and give the follow-up work to separate **resolution agents** — modular design through **separation of concerns**.
cards.explanation: Agents are not tied to one workflow: an Invoke agent node can reference an existing agent from the project. The shared categorization agent classifies requests in many workflows, while different resolution agents handle the follow-up actions. That separation of concerns makes workflows easier to maintain and to evolve over time.

cards.question: In a Microsoft Foundry workflow, which language do you write the conditions of If/Else nodes, the values of variables and the collections of For-each loops in?
cards.answer:
**Power Fx** — the low-code, Excel-like language that is the glue of a workflow; each **formula** is an expression that evaluates to a value:
- **If/Else** nodes evaluate a Power Fx condition to branch
- **Set variable** nodes compute values with it
- **For-each** nodes use it to iterate over a collection
cards.explanation: Power Fx lets a workflow manipulate data, evaluate conditions and control execution without complex code, so the flow reacts to user input, agent outputs or stored data. Typical decision point: check an agent's confidence score, then continue automatically or escalate to a human. Combined with variables and conditions, a For-each loop handles a list of inputs, such as several support tickets, without duplicating nodes or logic.

cards.question: Name the **two** kinds of variables that Power Fx formulas can reference in a Microsoft Foundry workflow.
cards.answer:
- **System variables** — context about the workflow or conversation: current activity, last message, user info
- **Local variables** — data captured or created during execution, used in later nodes
cards.explanation: System variables come from the platform; you read them to know where the conversation stands. Local variables are yours: a node stores a user's input or an agent's output in them, and later nodes reference them, for example `Local.Input` or `Local.Confidence > 0.8`. Referencing variables is what lets a workflow adapt to context and to the results of previous steps.

cards.question: Name **six** basic Power Fx formulas that a Microsoft Foundry workflow uses for **text values and conditions**, and what each returns.
cards.answer:
- **`Upper(Local.Input)`** — string to all caps
- **`Lower(Local.Input)`** — string to all lowercase
- **`Len(Local.Input)`** — number of characters
- **`Concatenate(Local.FirstName, " ", Local.LastName)`** — joins strings into one
- **`Local.Confidence > 0.8`** — conditional check, returns true/false
- **`If(Local.Confidence > 0.8, "Proceed", "Escalate")`** — returns one of two values
cards.explanation: The comparison and `If()` differ in what they return. A bare comparison yields true or false, which is exactly what an If/Else node needs to choose a branch. `If()` yields one of two values, so you use it where a value is wanted, such as setting a variable to "Proceed" or "Escalate" from the agent's confidence score.

cards.question: Name **six** basic Power Fx formulas that a Microsoft Foundry workflow uses for **lists, tables and empty values**, and what each returns.
cards.answer:
- **`Sum([10, 20, 30])`** — adds the numbers in a simple list
- **`Sum(Local.ItemList, Amount)`** — adds the `Amount` property of each record
- **`Count(Local.ItemList)`** — number of items
- **`IsBlank(Local.Input)`** — true if a variable or input is empty
- **`IsEmpty(Local.ItemList)`** — true if a table has no records
- **`ForAll(Local.ItemList, Upper(Name))`** — applies a formula to each item
cards.explanation: `Sum` takes either a plain list of numbers or a table plus the column to add up. `IsBlank` and `IsEmpty` are easy to mix up: `IsBlank` checks a single variable or input, `IsEmpty` checks whether a table holds any records. `ForAll` applies a formula to every item inside one expression, while a For-each node repeats whole workflow steps for each item.

cards.question: In a Microsoft Foundry workflow, an agent stores the open support tickets it found as a table in `Local.ItemList`. An If/Else node must skip the For-each loop when the table has **no records**. Which Power Fx formula do you use as the condition?
cards.answer: **`IsEmpty(Local.ItemList)`**
cards.explanation: `IsEmpty` returns true when a table has no records, and an If/Else node needs exactly such a true/false value to branch. `IsBlank` is the check for a single variable or input that is empty. `Count` and `Len` return numbers, not true or false.

options.why: Returns true if a table has no records, which is the condition the If/Else node needs.
IsBlank returns true if a single variable or input is empty; the check for a table without records is IsEmpty.
Count returns the number of items, a number rather than the true/false an If/Else condition needs.
Len returns the number of characters in a string, not whether a table holds any records.

cards.question: Name the **two** representations of a Microsoft Foundry workflow, what each is for, and how edits in one affect the other.
cards.answer:
- **Visual canvas** — conceptual understanding, tracing execution paths, collaborating
- **YAML** — textual form for advanced configuration, version tracking and source control
- **Kept in sync** — a change in either view is reflected in the other
cards.explanation: Both views show the same workflow definition. Pick the canvas when you need to see the flow or walk others through it. Pick YAML when you want text: fine-grained settings, diffs between versions, a source control repository. The visual designer generates the YAML, and you can download it from the portal into your codebase. Because edits flow both ways, analysts on the canvas and developers in YAML never drift apart.

cards.question: A change to a Microsoft Foundry workflow introduced errors. Which built-in feature lets you go back, and when does it record a version?
cards.answer:
- **Versioning**: every **save** creates a new, **immutable** version
- Review prior versions, compare changes, or **roll back** to an earlier one
cards.explanation: Versioning is the safety net for workflow changes. Because each saved version cannot change afterwards, an earlier working state is always there to compare against or restore. It also helps collaboration: the history shows who changed what and why. The workflow designer does not save automatically, so only what you save becomes a version — save regularly.

cards.question: Name the **four** best practices for refining and maintaining Microsoft Foundry workflows.
cards.answer:
- **Review for unused or redundant nodes** regularly
- **Handle structured agent outputs consistently**
- **Document decisions and logic with notes**
- **Use version history** to track changes and validate updates
cards.explanation: Maintenance is more than fixing errors; it improves clarity, reliability and efficiency. Notes are attached in the workflow visualizer to nodes or sections. They explain design decisions or clarify how a variable is used, so future maintainers understand the workflow's purpose and logic and make fewer errors. Combined with YAML editing and version control, this keeps workflows ready for enterprise use.

explanation_images.alt: A note beside the Triage-Agent node in the Foundry workflow visualizer, explaining that the agent categorizes tickets and stores the result in Local.TicketCategory.

cards.question: You designed and saved a workflow in the Microsoft Foundry portal and now want to run it from a Python backend. What are the steps?
cards.answer:
- Connect to the project with the **Azure AI Projects SDK** (`AIProjectClient`)
- Create a **conversation** (`openai_client.conversations.create()`)
- Call `openai_client.responses.create()` with the conversation id, the workflow referenced **by name** as an `agent_reference`, and the `input`
cards.explanation: The visual designer generates the workflow's YAML definition, and saving stores the workflow in the project. Code never rebuilds the workflow: it only names it. `AIProjectClient` handles authentication and gives access to the OpenAI-compatible API that runs conversations and workflows. The conversation is the context the workflow runs in. You can also download the YAML from the portal and keep it in your codebase.
cards.addition: Foundry retires workflows on December 1, 2026. New workflows should use Microsoft Agent Framework; the exported YAML definition is the portable artifact and keeps running when deployed as a hosted agent.

cards.question:
Complete the Python code that runs the Microsoft Foundry workflow `triage-workflow` and streams its events.

```python
conversation = openai_client.conversations.create()
stream = openai_client.___(
    conversation=conversation.id,
    extra_body={"agent": {"name": "triage-workflow", "type": "agent_reference"}},
    input="Users can't reset their password from the mobile app.",
    stream=True,
)
```
cards.answer: `responses.create` — a workflow runs through the **Responses API**, with the workflow named as an agent reference.
cards.explanation: The OpenAI-compatible client from the Foundry project executes the workflow through a response inside a conversation. The conversation is created first and only provides the context. The `extra_body` agent reference points the response at the saved workflow by name, so no model or workflow definition is passed in code. `stream=True` makes the call return events while the workflow runs.

options.why: The workflow is executed as a response in the conversation, with the workflow referenced in `extra_body`.
This call only creates the conversation context; it already ran in the line above and does not execute the workflow.
Chat Completions calls a model deployment directly and takes no conversation id or agent reference.
This is the older Assistants threads-and-runs API, not the conversation and responses calls Foundry workflows use.

cards.addition: `openai_client` comes from `project_client.get_openai_client()` on an `AIProjectClient` built with the project endpoint and an Entra ID credential such as `DefaultAzureCredential` (`pip install azure-ai-projects`).

cards.question: When you invoke a Microsoft Foundry workflow from code, what can the **`input`** parameter carry? Name the **four** kinds the course lists.
cards.answer:
- A **user question** that agents analyze and answer
- A **support ticket description** for classification and routing
- A **data payload** that triggers processing logic
- An **empty string** that just starts the workflow
cards.explanation: `input` is the prompt or message the workflow uses to drive its logic. Which kind fits depends on how the workflow is designed: a Q&A workflow expects a question, a triage workflow a ticket text, a processing workflow structured data. An empty string is also valid: it simply starts the workflow without specific input.

cards.question: Your Python app streams a Microsoft Foundry workflow run. Name the **two** common event types and what each signals.
cards.answer:
- **`response.completed`** — the workflow finished and returned its final response
- **`response.output_item.done`** — one output item finished, such as a **workflow action** (`ItemType.WORKFLOW_ACTION`)
cards.explanation: With streaming on, events arrive while the workflow runs. Use `response.output_item.done` to show real-time progress: when the item is a workflow action, read its `action_id` and `status`. Use `response.completed` to collect the result: loop over `event.response.output` and print each `output_text` content item. Events can also trigger external actions based on workflow state. Without streaming, you wait for the whole run and process only the final response.

cards.question: Your app runs a Microsoft Foundry workflow from Python. The workflow contains a human-in-the-loop step and pauses to wait for user input. How does the app resume it?
cards.answer: Send an **additional message to the same conversation** with the requested input; the workflow then continues.
cards.explanation: The conversation created before the first `responses.create` call holds the workflow's context. A human-in-the-loop pause means the workflow waits inside that conversation for input. The app supplies it as a further message to the same conversation, and execution resumes from where it stopped. Your app has to be ready to handle such pauses whenever the workflow design includes them.

options.text: Send an additional message with the input to the same conversation
options.why: A paused workflow resumes when the app sends more messages to its conversation with the requested input.

options.text: Create a new conversation and invoke the workflow again by name
options.why: A new conversation starts a fresh run without the paused run's context instead of resuming it.
Streaming only controls whether events arrive live or the final response at the end; it does not supply the requested input.

options.text: Edit the workflow's YAML definition and save a new version
options.why: Saving creates a new workflow version for future runs; it does not answer the question the running workflow is waiting on.

cards.question: Name the **five** scenarios the course lists for integrating Microsoft Foundry workflows into code, with the benefit of each.
cards.answer:
- **Web applications** — embed AI-driven workflows in user-facing apps
- **APIs and microservices** — expose workflow capabilities through REST endpoints
- **Batch processing** — invoke workflows programmatically for bulk operations
- **Testing and validation** — automate workflow testing in CI/CD pipelines
- **Custom interfaces** — build specialized UIs for specific workflow use cases
cards.explanation: All five rest on the same split: design and test the workflow visually in the Foundry portal, then call it by name from any software. Web apps and custom interfaces put the workflow in front of users. APIs and batch jobs run it behind the scenes, one request or many items at a time. Testing in CI/CD treats the workflow like any other component that must pass before release.

cards.question: You build a support-ticket triage workflow in the **Microsoft Foundry** workflow builder: one agent classifies each ticket, low-confidence tickets get a request for details, billing tickets are escalated, the rest get a drafted reply. Put the nodes in order.
cards.answer: **Set variable** → **For each** → triage **agent** → **If/Else** on confidence (Else: **Deliver a message**) → **If/Else** on category (Billing: escalation message) → resolution **agent**.
cards.explanation: The array of tickets must exist before the loop can walk over it. Inside the loop, the triage agent produces the JSON that both conditions read. The confidence check comes first: an unsure category should not decide the route. Only confident non-billing tickets reach the resolution agent. In the workflow actions menu, Set variable sits under **Data transformation**, Agent under **Invoke**, If/Else and For each under **Flow**, and Deliver a message under **Basics**.
items: Set variable (Data transformation): `Local.SupportTickets` holds the ticket array
For each (Flow): loop over `Local.SupportTickets` with the loop variable `CurrentTicket`
Agent (Invoke): Triage-Agent returns category and confidence as JSON
If/Else (Flow): `confidence > 0.6`; the Else branch delivers a message asking for details
If/Else (Flow): `category = "Billing"` delivers an escalation message
Else branch, Agent (Invoke): Resolution-Agent drafts the reply

cards.question: In a **Microsoft Foundry** workflow, an Invoke agent node classifies a ticket, and the next **If/Else** node must branch on the agent's confidence score. Which agent and node settings make that possible?
cards.answer:
- **Parameters** (agent Details) → Text format **JSON Schema** with a `confidence` field
- **Node settings** → **Input message**: `Local.CurrentTicket`
- **Save the output json_object as**: `TriageOutputJson`
- If/Else condition: `Local.TriageOutputJson.confidence > 0.6`
cards.explanation: A condition cannot read a field out of free text. The JSON Schema response format, saved with `strict: true`, makes the agent return `customer_issue`, `category` and `confidence` in a predictable shape. Node settings (unit 2.6.5 calls this area **Action settings**) store that object in a local variable, so later nodes address its fields with dot notation. The plain text reply is saved separately under **Save agent output message as**; the exercise feeds that text variable into the Resolution-Agent.

cards.question: Where in the **Microsoft Foundry** portal do you create a workflow, test it, and find the project endpoint to call it from Python?
cards.answer:
- Create: **Build** → **Agents** → **Workflows** tab → **Create** → **Blank workflow**
- Keep changes: **Save** in the visualizer
- Test: **Preview** → chat window
- Code: **Code** → **.env variables** → `AZURE_EXISTING_AIPROJECT_ENDPOINT`
cards.explanation: A blank workflow is the easy start even for a sequential flow, because you add exactly the nodes you need. Workflows are not saved automatically, so save before you preview. Preview runs the workflow in a chat: any message such as "Start processing support tickets." triggers it. Your code connects with `AIProjectClient` to that endpoint and invokes the workflow by the name you saved it under.

cards.question: Which node type would you use to handle multiple tickets in a workflow without duplicating nodes?
cards.answer: The **For-Each** node.
cards.explanation: For Each is a flow node in the Microsoft Foundry workflow designer. It uses Power Fx to iterate over a collection and runs the same set of actions for each item. Combined with variables and conditions, one loop handles a whole list of support tickets. Without it you would copy the same nodes once per ticket.

options.why: It branches execution on a condition; it runs once and does not loop over a list (2.6.4, 2.6.6).
It loops over a list of items and performs the same actions for each one, such as multiple support tickets (2.6.4, 2.6.6).
It is a basic chat node that sends a message to the user; it has no looping logic (2.6.4).

cards.question: Which of the following best describes how structured agent outputs are used in workflows?
cards.answer: They provide **predictable data** that can be stored in variables, evaluated with conditions, and trigger workflow steps.
cards.explanation: In a Microsoft Foundry workflow you define a response format such as a JSON schema on the Invoke agent node (Details tab). The output then follows a fixed shape. You store it in a variable via the node's Action settings. If/Else conditions and later agents read that variable, so the agent's answer decides the route. The flow nodes still do the routing; the output only feeds them.

options.text: They are ignored once generated, since agents always handle routing automatically
options.why: Routing comes from flow nodes such as If/Else that read the stored output; agents do not route the workflow by themselves (2.6.4, 2.6.5).

options.text: They provide predictable data that can be stored in variables, evaluated with conditions, and trigger workflow steps
options.why: A JSON schema gives the output a predictable shape, which is stored in a variable and drives routing logic and later nodes (2.6.5).

options.text: They replace the need for loops and If/Else nodes
options.why: Structured outputs feed the conditions of If/Else nodes and the variables loops work with; effective automation relies on the coordinated use of all node types (2.6.4, 2.6.6).

cards.question: The **Microsoft Agent Framework** is the next generation of which **two** earlier Microsoft frameworks?
cards.answer: **Semantic Kernel** and **AutoGen** — AutoGen's agent abstractions plus Semantic Kernel's enterprise features (session-based state, type safety, execution filters, telemetry), with new **graph-based workflows** on top.
cards.explanation: The same engineering teams built all three, and the new framework is the next generation of both. Graph-based workflows give developers explicit control over the execution paths of a multi-agent solution. Every agent derives from one unified `Agent` base class, so the interface stays the same whichever model provider sits underneath — the reason you can switch providers by changing only the client configuration, not the agent logic.

options.why: It contributes the enterprise features: session state, type safety, execution filters and telemetry.
It contributes the intuitive agent abstractions.
It is not a predecessor but the provider the framework connects to — the recommended one for production.
Prompt flow is a different Microsoft tool for building LLM app flows; the Agent Framework succeeds only Semantic Kernel and AutoGen.

cards.question: Name the **seven** composable building blocks (key features) of the **Microsoft Agent Framework**.
cards.answer:
- **Model clients** — unified interface to multiple AI providers
- **Agent session** — native state for multi-turn context
- **Context providers** — plug-and-play memory surfacing relevant information
- **Function tools** — custom functions, auto-registered with generated schema
- **MCP clients** — Model Context Protocol, tool discovery at runtime
- **Middleware** — hooks to intercept, log or modify agent actions
- **Workflow orchestration** — graph-based sequential, concurrent, group chat, handoff
cards.explanation: Instead of wiring separate libraries for memory, tool integration and model access by hand, the framework bundles them as blocks you use alone or combine as the solution grows. The pairs to keep apart: the agent session holds the conversation itself, context providers add relevant memory to it. Function tools are functions you register up front, MCP clients discover tools at runtime. Middleware hooks run before and after an agent's actions, workflow orchestration controls the path across several agents.

cards.question: Name the **five** capabilities every agent in the **Microsoft Agent Framework** supports out of the box, whatever provider powers it.
cards.answer:
- **Function calling** — automatically invoke registered tools for external APIs and services
- **Multi-turn conversations** — chat history kept locally or by the service
- **Structured outputs** — type-safe, schema-validated responses
- **Streaming responses** — results arrive incrementally as generated
- **Service-provided tools** — built-in code execution, file search, web search where the provider supports them
cards.explanation: All agents share the same `Agent` base class, so these capabilities do not depend on provider-specific APIs and you write application logic once. Two of them still depend on the provider: where the chat history lives (local or service-side) and which built-in tools exist. Function calling uses tools you register yourself; service-provided tools are hosted and run by the provider.

cards.question: Which **Microsoft Agent Framework** providers offer **service chat history**, and which do not?
cards.answer:
- **Yes:** **Foundry Agent Service**, **Azure OpenAI Responses**, **OpenAI Responses**
- **No:** **Azure OpenAI Chat Completion**, **OpenAI Chat Completion**, **Anthropic Claude**, **Amazon Bedrock**, **GitHub Copilot**, **Ollama** (OpenAI-compatible)
cards.explanation: The pattern to remember: the Foundry Agent Service and the two Responses APIs keep history on the service side. The two Chat Completion APIs and the other providers (Anthropic Claude, Amazon Bedrock, GitHub Copilot, Ollama) do not, so the framework keeps the conversation locally in the session. Because all providers sit behind the same interface, you can switch between them as models or requirements change — only the client configuration changes, not the agent logic.

cards.question: You build a production agent with the **Microsoft Agent Framework** and must keep conversation context across turns without managing that state yourself. Which provider is recommended, and why?
cards.answer: The **Foundry Agent Service** — its **service-side chat history** persists the agent session across turns automatically.
cards.explanation: You connect to the Foundry project by authenticating with your Azure credentials, then create agents that use the Agent Service's capabilities. Beyond persistent chat history these are dynamic tool discovery through Model Context Protocol (MCP) tool support and integration with Azure services. That combination is why the course calls Foundry the recommended provider for production scenarios where keeping context is critical.

cards.question: Put the steps in order to build and talk to a Foundry agent with the **Microsoft Agent Framework** in Python.
cards.answer: Foundry project with a deployed model → **DefaultAzureCredential** → **Foundry chat client** → agent with instructions → **session** → send messages.
cards.explanation: Code can only start once a project and a model deployment exist. The credential comes before the client because the client needs it. The **Foundry chat client** is the bridge to the Foundry Agent Service: it handles authentication, request routing and service-side session management. The agent is created from that client. Only the **session** then holds the conversation: its execution method processes the prompt, coordinates any tool calls and returns the model's response.
items: Set up a Microsoft Foundry project with a deployed model
Configure authentication with DefaultAzureCredential
Initialize the Foundry chat client with credential, project endpoint and model name
Create the agent from the chat client with instructions and optional tools
Open a session on the agent and send user messages to it

cards.question: Name the **five** inputs you provide with the **Microsoft Agent Framework** to connect a Foundry chat client to your Microsoft Foundry project and create an agent on it.
cards.answer:
- **Credential** — `DefaultAzureCredential`: Azure CLI login in dev, managed identity in production; no keys in code
- **Project endpoint** — the URL of the Foundry project
- **Model deployment name** — the deployed model the agent uses
- **Instructions** — system prompt: role, goals, constraints
- **Tools** (optional) — custom functions the agent can call
cards.explanation: The first three go into the Foundry chat client; the last two define the agent. `DefaultAzureCredential` resolves the right credential for the environment by itself, so the same code runs on a developer laptop and in production without a hardcoded connection string or API key. For tools, the framework registers them and generates their schemas automatically, so the model knows when and how to call each one.
cards.addition: Current Python shape: `Agent(client=FoundryChatClient(project_endpoint=..., model=..., credential=...), instructions=...)`. The docs also advise a specific credential such as `ManagedIdentityCredential` in production instead of `DefaultAzureCredential`.

cards.question: A **Microsoft Agent Framework** session can keep conversation history in **two** ways. Name them. Which one lets a conversation continue after your app restarts or scales out to several instances?
cards.answer:
- **Persistent history** — service-side storage in the Foundry Agent Service; survives restarts and scale-out
- **Local history** — in memory in the session object, for providers without service-side history; lost on process restart
cards.explanation: One call to the agent's run method is one exchange: one message, one response. The **session** is what remembers the earlier turns. With the Foundry provider, the history lives in the service, not in your application's memory, so any instance can pick the conversation up. Local history suits short-lived or stateless apps. Service-side history is one reason the Foundry Agent Service is the recommended provider for production.
cards.addition: In Python the session is an `AgentSession`: create it with `session = agent.create_session()` and pass it on every turn with `await agent.run("…", session=session)`.

cards.question: Name the **two** response modes of a **Microsoft Agent Framework** agent's run method. Which one fits a chat UI that should show the answer while the model is still generating it, and which property gives you the final text in both modes?
cards.answer:
- **Non-streaming (synchronous)** — waits, then returns one complete response object
- **Streaming (asynchronous)** — returns a response stream you iterate asynchronously, with partial updates; the choice for the chat UI
- **`text` property** — aggregates all text content of the output, in both modes
cards.explanation: Non-streaming is the simplest pattern and works when output need not appear step by step. Streaming suits user-facing interfaces because text shows up progressively instead of after a wait. Because the response exposes `text` either way, switching modes does not change how you extract the final answer.
cards.addition: In Python, `await agent.run("…")` returns an `AgentResponse`. `agent.run("…", stream=True)` returns a `ResponseStream`; iterate it with `async for update in …` and read `update.text`.

cards.question: In the Microsoft Agent Framework, which **two** broad categories of tools can an agent use, who executes each, and how can another agent become one of its tools?
cards.answer:
- **Service-provided tools** — hosted by the provider; you enable them in the agent configuration and the provider executes them
- **Custom function tools** — your own Python functions, passed to the agent at creation; the framework generates their schema and runs them
- An inner **agent** can itself be converted into a function tool for an outer agent
cards.explanation: Without tools an agent can only produce text from what it already knows; tools let it call APIs, run code or search files. You can register several tools in one list, and the model picks the right one from the conversation and the tool descriptions — no routing logic needed. Wrapping a specialised agent as a tool lets a coordinating agent delegate to it, a modular design that leads into multi-agent orchestration.

cards.question: Name the **six** commonly used service-provided tools a Microsoft Agent Framework agent gets with the Foundry provider.
cards.answer:
- **Code Interpreter** — sandboxed Python for calculations and data analysis
- **File Search** — retrieves information from uploaded documents
- **Web Search** — up-to-date internet information
- **Hosted MCP Tools** — MCP servers invoked by the provider runtime
- **Azure AI Search** — queries an index through a Foundry connection
- **Foundry Toolboxes** — named, versioned bundles of hosted tool configurations in a Foundry project
cards.explanation: None of these needs your own implementation: you list them in the agent configuration and the provider executes them. Pick by the data source — computation goes to Code Interpreter, your uploaded files to File Search, live public information to Web Search, an existing search index to Azure AI Search. Some, such as Azure AI Search, Bing Grounding and SharePoint, are preview or experimental and may have limited support on providers other than Foundry.

cards.question: In the Microsoft Agent Framework, what are the **two** ways to describe a Python function so the model can call it reliably as a tool?
cards.answer:
- **Type annotations** — `Annotated` with a description on each parameter; the **docstring** becomes the tool description
- **`@tool` decorator** — name and description given as decorator arguments; optionally an explicit **Pydantic** schema for the input
cards.explanation: The framework inspects the function signature and generates a schema telling the model what the function does, which parameters it expects and what it returns. Annotations are the lightweight route; the decorator gives full control over what the model sees. Either way, when the model decides to call the tool, the framework executes the function and hands the result back to the model before the final response is generated.

cards.question: A Microsoft Agent Framework agent has a function tool that issues customer refunds. A person must confirm each refund before the function runs. What do you configure?
cards.answer: **Tool approval** — set `approval_mode` on that function's `@tool` decorator.
cards.explanation: With approval mode enabled, the agent pauses before calling the function and asks for confirmation. It fits actions that are irreversible, expensive or touch sensitive data. Because it is set per tool, harmless tools such as lookups keep running without interruption while only the risky one waits for a human.
cards.addition: To require approval, set `approval_mode="always_require"` (`"never_require"` skips it). The run then returns `user_input_requests`; answer each with `to_function_approval_response(True or False)` and run again in the same session.

options.why: Tool approval makes the agent pause before that specific function and request human confirmation.

options.text: Add "always ask the user before refunding" to the agent's instructions
options.why: Instructions only steer the model; nothing stops it from calling the function, so confirmation is not enforced.

options.text: Bundle the refund function into a Foundry Toolbox
options.why: A Foundry Toolbox is a named, versioned bundle of hosted tool configurations, not an approval mechanism.

options.text: Register a context provider on the agent
options.why: Context providers are memory components that surface relevant information to the agent, not approval gates.

cards.question: Name the **five** best practices for writing custom function tools for an AI agent in the Microsoft Agent Framework.
cards.answer:
- **Write clear descriptions** — what the function does and when to use it
- **Annotate every parameter** — so the model can build valid calls
- **Return meaningful data** — structured, interpretable output
- **Keep tools focused** — one thing per tool
- **Handle errors gracefully** — return an informative error message instead of raising
cards.explanation: The model only sees the descriptions, so its choice of tool depends entirely on them, and unclear parameter names lead to invalid calls. The return value goes straight into the model's answer, so it must be readable. A function with several responsibilities is hard to invoke correctly. An exception gives the model nothing to work with; an error message lets it respond helpfully when input is unexpected or an external service fails.

cards.question: Without leaving Visual Studio Code, you set up a Microsoft Foundry project and a model deployment for a Microsoft Agent Framework app. Put the steps in order, from the extension to the app's `.env` file.
cards.answer: **Foundry Toolkit** extension → **Create Project** → **Model Catalog** > **Deploy** → deployment settings > **Deploy to Microsoft Foundry** → **Copy Project Endpoint** → endpoint and deployment name into `.env`.
cards.explanation: The Foundry Toolkit extension lets you work with Foundry project resources from VS Code instead of the Foundry portal; older labels still call it **AI Toolkit**. If a default project is already active, right-click it > **Switch Default Project** to create another. The Model Catalog also opens from the **+** next to **Models** or with **F1** > **Foundry Toolkit: Show model catalog**. The finished deployment appears under **Models**. The app needs two values from this setup: the project endpoint and the deployment name.
